We have supplies ready in all our wants (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.32">v. 32</reference>): <hi type="italic">He that spared,</hi> &c. Who can be against us, to strip us, to deprive us of our comforts? Who can cut off our streams, while we have a fountain to go to? 1. Observe what God has done for us, on which our hopes are built: <hi type="italic">He spared not his own Son.</hi> When he was to undertake our salvation, the Father was willing to part with him, did not think him too precious a gift to bestow for the salvation of poor souls; now we may know that he loves us, in that he hath not withheld his Son, his own Son, his only Son, from us, as he said of Abraham, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.12">Gen. xxii. 12</reference>. If nothing less will save man, rather than man shall perish let him go, though it were out of his bosom. Thus did he <hi type="italic">deliver him up for us all,</hi> that is, for all the elect; <hi type="italic">for us all,</hi> not only for our good, but in our stead, as a sacrifice of atonement to be a propitiation for sin. When he had undertaken it, he did not spare him. Though he was his own Son, yet, being made sin for us, it pleased the Lord to bruise him. <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Ouk epheisato</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">he did not abate</hi> him a farthing of that great debt, but charged it home. <hi type="italic">Awake, O sword.</hi> He did not <hi type="italic">spare his own Son that served him,</hi> that he might spare us, though we have done him so much disservice. 2. What we may therefore expect he will do: He will <hi type="italic">with him freely give us all things.</hi> (1.) It is implied that he will give us Christ, for other things are bestowed with him: not only with him given for us, but with him given to us. He that put himself to so much charge to make the purchase for us surely will not hesitate at making the application to us. (2.) He will with him freely give us all things, all things that he sees to be needful and necessary for us, all good things, and more we should not desire, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.10">Ps. xxxiv. 10</reference>. And Infinite Wisdom shall be the judge whether it be good for us and needful for us or no. <hi type="italic">Freely give</hi>—freely, without reluctancy; he is ready to give, meets us with his favours;—and freely, without recompence, without money, and without price. <hi type="italic">How shall he not?</hi> Can it be imagined that he should do the greater and not do the less? that he should give so great a gift for us when we were enemies, and should deny us any good thing, now that through him we are friends and children? Thus may we by faith argue against our fears of want. He that hath prepared a crown and kingdom for us will be sure to give us enough to bear our charges in the way to it. He that hath designed us for the inheritance of sons when we come to age will not let us want necessaries in the mean time. <div eID="gen30670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30671" type="x-p"/> II. We have an answer ready to all accusations and a security against all condemnations (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.33-Rom.8.34">v. 33, 34</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who shall lay any thing?</hi> Doth the law accuse them? Do their own consciences accuse them? Is the devil, the accuser of the brethren, accusing them before our God day and night? This is enough to answer all those accusations, <hi type="italic">It is God that justifieth.</hi> Men may justify themselves, as the Pharisees did, and yet the accusations may be in full force against them; but, if God justifies, this answers all. He is the judge, the king, the party offended, and his judgment is according to truth, and sooner or later all the world will be brought to be of his mind; so that we may challenge all our accusers to come and put in their charge. This overthrows them all; it is God, the righteous faithful God, that justifieth. <hi type="italic">Who is he that condemneth?</hi> Though they cannot make good the charge yet they will be ready to condemn; but we have a plea ready to move in arrest of judgment, a plea which cannot be overruled. <hi type="italic">It is Christ that died,</hi> &c. It is by virtue of our interest in Christ, our relation to him, and our union with him, that we are thus secured. 1. His death: <hi type="italic">It is Christ that died.</hi> By the merit of his death he paid our debt; and the surety's payment is a good plea to an action of debt. It is Christ, an able all-sufficient Saviour. 2. His resurrection: <hi type="italic">Yea, rather, that has risen again.</hi> This is a much greater encouragement, for it is a convincing evidence that divine justice was satisfied by the merit of his death. His resurrection was his acquittance, it was a legal discharge. Therefore the apostle mentions it with a <hi type="italic">yea, rather.</hi> If he had died, and not risen again, we had been where we were. 3. His sitting at the right hand of God: He is <hi type="italic">even at the right hand of God</hi>—a further evidence that he has done his work, and a mighty encouragement to us in reference to all accusations, that we have a friend, such a friend, in court. At <hi type="italic">the right hand of God,</hi> which denotes that he is ready there—always at hand; and that he is ruling there—all power is given to him. Our friend is himself the judge. 4. The intercession which he makes there. He is there, not unconcerned about us, not forgetful of us, but <hi type="italic">making intercession.</hi> He is agent for us there, an advocate for us, to answer all accusations, to put in our plea, and to prosecute it with effect, to appear for us and to present our petitions. And is not this abundant matter for comfort? What shall we say to these things? Is this the manner of men, O Lord God? What room is left for doubting and disquietment? Why art thou cast down, O my soul? Some understand the accusation and condemnation here spoken of of that which the suffering saints met with from men. The primitive Christians had many black crimes laid to their charge—heresy, sedition, rebellion, and what not? For these the ruling powers condemned them: "But no matter for that" (says the apostle); "while we stand right at God's bar it is of no great moment how we stand at men's. To all the hard censures, the malicious calumnies, and the unjust and unrighteous sentences of men, we may with comfort oppose our justification before God through Christ Jesus as that which doth abundantly countervail," <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.3-1Cor.4.4">1 Cor. iv. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen30671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30672" type="x-p"/> III. We have good assurance of our preservation and continuance in this blessed state, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.35-Rom.8.39">v. 35, to the end</reference>. The fears of the saints lest they should lose their hold of Christ are often very discouraging and disquieting, and create them a great deal of disturbance; but here is that which may silence their fears, and still such storms, that nothing can separate them. We have here from the apostle, <div eID="gen30672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30673" type="x-p"/> 1. A daring challenge to all the enemies of the saints to separate them, if they could, from the love of Christ. <hi type="italic">Who shall?</hi> None shall, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.35-Rom.8.37">v. 35-37</reference>. God having manifested his love in giving his own Son for us, and not hesitating at that, can we imagine that any thing else should divert or dissolve that love? Observe here, <div eID="gen30673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30674" type="x-p"/> (1.) The present calamities of Christ's beloved ones supposed—that they meet with <hi type="italic">tribulation</hi> on all hands, are in <hi type="italic">distress,</hi> know not which way to look for any succour and relief in this world, are followed with <hi type="italic">persecution</hi> from an angry malicious world that always hated those whom Christ loved, pinched with <hi type="italic">famine,</hi> and starved with <hi type="italic">nakedness,</hi> when stripped of all <hi type="italic">creature-comforts,</hi> exposed to the greatest <hi type="italic">perils,</hi> the <hi type="italic">sword</hi> of the magistrate drawn against them, ready to be sheathed in their bowels, bathed in their blood. Can a case be supposed more black and dismal? It is illustrated (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.36">v. 36</reference>) by a passage quoted from <reference osisRef="Ps.44.22">Ps. xliv. 22</reference>, <hi type="italic">For thy sake we are killed all the day long,</hi> which intimates that we are not to think strange, no not concerning the fiery bloody trial. We see the Old-Testament saints had the same lot; so persecuted they the prophets that were before us. <hi type="italic">Killed all the day long,</hi> that is, continually exposed to and expecting the fatal stroke. There is still every day, and all the day long, one or other of the people of God bleeding and dying under the rage of persecuting enemies. <hi type="italic">Accounted as sheep for the slaughter;</hi> they make no more of killing a Christian than of butchering a sheep. Sheep are killed, not because they are hurtful while they live, but because they are useful when they are dead. They kill the Christians to please themselves, to be food to their malice. <hi type="italic">They eat up my people as they eat bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Ps. xiv. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen30674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30675" type="x-p"/> (2.) The inability of all these things to separate us from the love of Christ. Shall they, can they, do it? No, by no means. All this will not cut the bond of love and friendship that is between Christ and true believers. [1.] Christ doth not, will not, love us the less for all this. All these troubles are very consistent with the strong and constant love of the Lord Jesus. They are neither a cause nor an evidence of the abatement of his love. When Paul was whipped, and beaten, and imprisoned, and stoned, did Christ love him ever the less? Were his favours intermitted? his smiles any whit suspended? his visits more shy? By no means, but the contrary. These things separate us from the love of other friends. When Paul was brought before Nero all men forsook him, but then the Lord stood by him, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.16-2Tim.4.17">2 Tim. iv. 16, 17</reference>. Whatever persecuting enemies may rob us of, they cannot rob us of the love of Christ, they cannot intercept his love-tokens, they cannot interrupt nor exclude his visits: and therefore, let them do their worst, they cannot make a true believer miserable. [2.] We do not, will not, love him the less for this; and that for this reason, because we do not think that he loves us the less. Charity thinks no evil, entertains no misgiving thoughts, makes no hard conclusions, no unkind constructions, takes all in good part that comes from love. A true Christian loves Christ never the less though he suffer for him, thinks never the worse of Christ through he lose all for him. <div eID="gen30675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30676" type="x-p"/> (3.) The triumph of believers in this ( <reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">v. 37</reference>): <hi type="italic">Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors.</hi> <div eID="gen30676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30677" type="x-p"/> [1.] We are conquerors: though killed all the day long, yet conquerors. A strange way of conquering, but it was Christ's way; thus he triumphed over principalities and powers in his cross. It is a surer and a nobler way of conquest by faith and patience than by fire and sword. The enemies have sometimes confessed themselves baffled and overcome by the invincible courage and constancy of the martyrs, who thus overcame the most victorious princes by not loving their lives to the death, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.11">Rev. xii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen30677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30678" type="x-p"/> [2.] We are more than conquerors. In our patiently bearing these trials we are not only conquerors, but more than conquerors, that is, triumphers. Those are more than conquerors that conquer, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> With little loss. Many conquests are dearly bought; but what do the suffering saints lose? Why, they lose that which the gold loses in the furnace, nothing but the dross. It is no great loss to lose things which are not—a body that is of the earth, earthy. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> With great gain. The spoils are exceedingly rich; glory, honour, and peace, a crown of righteousness that fades not away. In this the suffering saints have triumphed; not only have not been separated from the love of Christ, but have been taken into the most sensible endearments and embraces of it. As afflictions abound, consolations much more abound, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2 Cor. i. 5</reference>. There is one more than a conqueror, when pressed above measure. He that embraced the stake, and said, "Welcome the cross of Christ, welcome everlasting life,"—he that dated his letter from the delectable orchard of the Leonine prison,—he that said, "In these flames I feel no more pain than if I were upon a bed of down,"—she who, a little before her martyrdom, being asked how she did, said, "Well and merry, and going to heaven,"—those that have gone smiling to the stake, and stood singing in the flames—these were more than conquerors. <div eID="gen30678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30679" type="x-p"/> [3.] It is only <hi type="italic">through Christ that loved us,</hi> the merit of his death taking the sting out of all these troubles, the Spirit of his grace strengthening us, and enabling us to bear them with holy courage and constancy, and coming in with special comforts and supports. Thus we are conquerors, not in our own strength, but in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. We are conquerors by virtue of our interest in Christ's victory. He hath overcome the world for us (<reference osisRef="John.16.33">John xvi. 33</reference>), both the good things and the evil things of it; so that we have nothing to do but to pursue the victory, and to divide the spoil, and so are more than conquerors. <div eID="gen30679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30680" type="x-p"/> 2. A direct and positive conclusion of the whole matter: <hi type="italic">For I am persuaded,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.38-Rom.8.39">v. 38, 39</reference>. It denotes a full, and strong, and affectionate persuasion, arising from the experience of the strength and sweetness of the divine love. And here he enumerates all those things which might be supposed likely to separate between Christ and believers, and concludes that it could not be done. (1.) <hi type="italic">Neither death nor life</hi>—neither the terrors of death on the one hand nor the comforts and pleasures of life on the other, neither the fear of death nor the hope of life. Or, We shall not be separated from that love either in death or in life. (2.) <hi type="italic">Nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers.</hi> Both the good angels and the bad are called principalities and powers: the good, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.21">Eph. i. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.1.16">Col. i. 16</reference>; the bad, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Eph. vi. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col. ii. 15</reference>. And neither shall do it. The good angels will not, the bad shall not; and neither can. The good angels are engaged friends, the bad are restrained enemies. (3.) <hi type="italic">Nor things present, nor things to come</hi>—neither the sense of troubles present nor the fear of troubles to come. Time shall not separate us, eternity shall not. Things present separate us from things to come, and things to come separate and cut us off from things present; but neither from the love of Christ, whose favour is twisted in with both present things and things to come. (4.) <hi type="italic">Nor height, nor depth</hi>—neither the height of prosperity and preferment, nor the depth of adversity and disgrace; nothing from heaven above, no storms, no tempests; nothing on earth below, no rocks, no seas, no dungeons. (5.) <hi type="italic">Nor any other creature</hi>—any thing that can be named or thought of. It will not, it cannot, separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. It cannot cut off or impair our love to God, or God's to us; nothing does it, can do it, but sin. Observe, The love that exists between God and true believers is through Christ. He is the Mediator of our love: it is in and through him that God can love us and that we dare love God. This is the ground of the stedfastness of the love; therefore God rests in his love (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zeph. iii. 17</reference>), because Jesus Christ, in whom he loves us, is the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever. <div eID="gen30680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30681" type="x-p"/> Mr. Hugh Kennedy, an eminent Christian of Ayr, in Scotland, when he was dying, called for a Bible; but, finding his sight gone, he said, "Turn me to the eighty of the Romans, and set my finger at these words, <hi type="italic">I am persuaded that neither death nor life,</hi>" &c. "Now," said he, "is my finger upon them?" And, when they told him it was, without speaking any more, he said, "Now, God be with you, my children; I have breakfasted with you, and shall sup with my Lord Jesus Christ this night;" and so departed.  <chapter eID="Rom.8"/> <div eID="gen30681" type="x-p"/>

entries.1d493083cfe29fd311201ad0dd0c08b803293685: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16498"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 8</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Rom.8.1-Rom.8.39">Ro 8:1-39</reference>. Conclusion of the Whole Argument--The Glorious Completeness of Them That Are in Christ Jesus.</title> <div sID="gen32124" type="x-p"/> In this surpassing chapter the several streams of the preceding argument meet and flow in one "river of the water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb," until it seems to lose itself in the ocean of a blissful eternity.<div eID="gen32124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32125" type="x-p"/> First: The Sanctification of Believers (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.1-Rom.8.13">Ro 8:1-13</reference>).<div eID="gen32125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32126" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16498"/><hi type="bold">1. There is therefore now, &c.--</hi>referring to the immediately preceding context [Olshausen, Philippi, Meyer, Alford, &c.]. The subject with which the seventh chapter concludes is still under consideration. The scope of <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1-Rom.8.4">Ro 8:1-4</reference> is to show how "the law of sin and death" is deprived of its power to bring believers again into bondage, and how the holy law of God receives in them the homage of a living obedience [Calvin, Fraser, Philippi, Meyer, Alford, &c.].<div eID="gen32126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32127" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no condemnation: to them which are in Christ Jesus--</hi>As Christ, who "knew no sin," was, to all legal effects, "made sin for us," so are we, who believe in Him, to all legal effects, "made the righteousness of God in Him" (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>); and thus, one with Him in the divine reckoning. there is to such "NO CONDEMNATION." (Compare <reference osisRef="John.3.18">Joh 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.24">5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.18">Ro 5:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.19">19</reference>). But this is no mere legal arrangement: it is a union in life; believers, through the indwelling of Christ's Spirit in them, having one life with Him, as truly as the head and the members of the same body have one life.<div eID="gen32127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32128" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit--</hi>The evidence of manuscripts seems to show that this clause formed no part of the original text of this verse, but that the first part of it was early introduced, and the second later, from <reference osisRef="Rom.8.4">Ro 8:4</reference>, probably as an explanatory comment, and to make the transition to <reference osisRef="Rom.8.2">Ro 8:2</reference> easier. <div eID="gen32128" type="x-p"/>
entries.8956a29b6fda7716bd52fd406687c29bad5e54d8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16499"/><div sID="gen32129" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16499"/><hi type="bold">2. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free--</hi>rather, "freed me"--referring to the time of his conversion, when first he believed.<div eID="gen32129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32130" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the law of sin and death--</hi>It is the Holy Ghost who is here called "the Spirit of life," as opening up in the souls of believers a fountain of spiritual life (see on <reference osisRef="John.7.38">Joh 7:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.39">39</reference>); just as He is called "the Spirit of truth," as "guiding them into all truth" (<reference osisRef="John.16.13">Joh 16:13</reference>), and "the Spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord" (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.2">Is 11:2</reference>), as the inspirer of these qualities. And He is called "the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus," because it is as members of Christ that He takes up His abode in believers, who in consequence of this have one life with their Head. And as the word "law" here has the same meaning as in <reference osisRef="Rom.7.23">Ro 7:23</reference>, namely, "an inward principle of action, operating with the fixedness and regularity of a law," it thus appears that "the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus" here means, "that new principle of action which the Spirit of Christ has opened up within us--the law of our new being." This "sets us free," as soon as it takes possession of our inner man, "from the law of sin and death" that is, from the enslaving power of that corrupt principle which carries death in its bosom. The "strong man armed" is overpowered by the "stronger than he"; the weaker principle is dethroned and expelled by the more powerful; the principle of spiritual life prevails against and brings into captivity the principle of spiritual death--"leading captivity captive." If this be the apostle's meaning, the whole verse is to this effect: That the triumph of believers over their inward corruption, through the power of Christ's Spirit in them, proves them to be in Christ Jesus, and as such absolved from condemnation. But this is now explained more fully. <div eID="gen32130" type="x-p"/>
entries.6248af2cedaceacb908774da8eea7de2c22c71dc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16500"/><div sID="gen32131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16500"/><hi type="bold">3-4. For what the law could not do, &c.--</hi>a difficult and much controverted verse. But it is clearly, we think, the law's inability to free us from the dominion of sin that the apostle has in view; as has partly appeared already (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.8.2">Ro 8:2</reference>), and will more fully appear presently. The law could irritate our sinful nature into more virulent action, as we have seen in <reference osisRef="Rom.7.5">Ro 7:5</reference>, but it could not secure its own fulfilment. How that is accomplished comes now to be shown.<div eID="gen32131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in that it was weak through the flesh--</hi>that is, having to address itself to us through a corrupt nature, too strong to be influenced by mere commands and threatenings.<div eID="gen32132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God, &c.--</hi>The sentence is somewhat imperfect in its structure, which occasions a certain obscurity. The meaning is, that whereas the law was powerless to secure its own fulfilment for the reason given, God took the method now to be described for attaining that end.<div eID="gen32133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32134" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sending--</hi>"having sent"<div eID="gen32134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his own Son--</hi>This and similar expressions plainly imply that Christ was God's "OWN Son" before He was sent--that is, in His own proper Person, and independently of His mission and appearance in the flesh (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.8.32">Ro 8:32</reference> and <reference osisRef="Gal.4.4">Ga 4:4</reference>); and if so, He not only has the very nature of God, even as a son of his father, but is essentially of the Father, though in a sense too mysterious for any language of ours properly to define (see on the first through fourth chapters). And this peculiar relationship is put forward here to enhance the greatness and define the nature of the relief provided, as coming from beyond the precincts of sinful humanity altogether, yea, immediately from the Godhead itself.<div eID="gen32135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the likeness of sinful flesh--</hi>literally, "of the flesh of sin"; a very remarkable and pregnant expression. He was made in the reality of our flesh, but only in the likeness of its sinful condition. He took our nature as it is in us, compassed with infirmities, with nothing to distinguish Him as man from sinful men, save that He was without sin. Nor does this mean that He took our nature with all its properties save one; for sin is no property of humanity at all, but only the disordered state of our souls, as the fallen family of Adam; a disorder affecting, indeed, and overspreading our entire nature, but still purely our own.<div eID="gen32136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32137" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and for sin--</hi>literally, "and about sin"; that is, "on the business of sin." The expression is purposely a general one, because the design was not to speak of Christ's mission to atone for sin, but in virtue of that atonement to destroy its dominion and extirpate it altogether from believers. We think it wrong, therefore, to render the words (as in the Margin) "by a sacrifice for sin" (suggested by the language of the Septuagint and approved by Calvin, &c.); for this sense is too definite, and makes the idea of expiation more prominent than it is.<div eID="gen32137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">condemned sin--</hi>"condemned it to lose its power over men" [Beza, Bengel, Fraser, Meyer, Tholuck, Philippi, Alford]. In this glorious sense our Lord says of His approaching death (<reference osisRef="John.12.31">Joh 12:31</reference>), "Now is the judgment of this world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out," and again (see on <reference osisRef="John.16.11">Joh 16:11</reference>), "When He (the Spirit) shall come, He shall convince the world of ... judgment, because the prince of this world is judged," that is, condemned to let go his hold of men, who, through the Cross, shall be emancipated into the liberty and power to be holy.<div eID="gen32138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the flesh--</hi>that is, in human nature, henceforth set free from the grasp of sin. <div eID="gen32139" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc9ce8d09636c7739aaf6c10a3ad7f909a5216e9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16502"/><div sID="gen32145" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16502"/><hi type="bold">5. For they that are after the flesh--</hi>that is, under the influence of the fleshly principle.<div eID="gen32145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32146" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do mind--</hi>give their attention to (<reference osisRef="Phil.3.19">Php 3:19</reference>).<div eID="gen32146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the things of the flesh, &c.--</hi>Men must be under the predominating influence of one or other of these two principles, and, according as the one or the other has the mastery, will be the complexion of their life, the character of their actions. <div eID="gen32147" type="x-p"/>
entries.f111147569b20afa28d74096902b8bd1056f24f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16503"/><div sID="gen32148" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16503"/><hi type="bold">6. For--</hi>a mere particle of transition here [Tholuck], like "but" or "now."<div eID="gen32148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be carnally minded--</hi>literally, "the mind" or "minding of the flesh" (Margin); that is, the pursuit of fleshly ends.<div eID="gen32149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is death--</hi>not only "ends in" [Alford, &c.], but even now "is"; carrying death into its bosom, so that such are "dead while they live" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.6">1Ti 5:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.1">Ep 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>) [Philippi].<div eID="gen32150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but to be spiritually minded--</hi>"the mind" or "minding of the spirit"; that is, the pursuit of spiritual objects.<div eID="gen32151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is life and peace--</hi>not "life" only, in contrast with the "death" that is in the other pursuit, but "peace"; it is the very element of the soul's deepest repose and true bliss. <div eID="gen32152" type="x-p"/>
entries.d228e2c824515928b375a309bc9c6b8ff09b5e8c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16504"/><div sID="gen32153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16504"/><hi type="bold">7. Because the carnal mind is enmity against God--</hi>The desire and pursuit of carnal ends is a state of enmity to God, wholly incompatible with true life and peace in the soul.<div eID="gen32153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for it is not subject--</hi>"doth not submit itself."<div eID="gen32154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to the law of God, neither indeed can be--</hi>In such a state of mind there neither is nor can be the least subjection to the law of God. Many things may be done which the law requires, but nothing either is or can be done because God's law requires it, or purely to please God. <div eID="gen32155" type="x-p"/>
entries.0076155f6dc747daa5f48b6aa85480111d216570: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16505"/><div sID="gen32156" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16505"/><hi type="bold">8. So then--</hi>nearly equivalent to "And so."<div eID="gen32156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they that are in--</hi>and, therefore, under the government of<div eID="gen32157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the flesh cannot please God--</hi>having no obediential principle, no desire to please Him. <div eID="gen32158" type="x-p"/>
entries.1248707e9af1cf890e828e3a0ce344f164bd0b51: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16506"/><div sID="gen32159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16506"/><hi type="bold">9. But ye are not in the flesh, but in the spirit, if so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you--</hi>This does not mean, "if the disposition or mind of God dwell in you"; but "if the Holy Ghost dwell in you" (see <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.11">1Co 6:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.16">3:16</reference>, &c.). (It thus appears that to be "in the spirit" means here to be under the dominion of our own renewed mind; because the indwelling of God's Spirit is given as the evidence that we are "in the spirit").<div eID="gen32159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Now--</hi>"But."<div eID="gen32160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if any man have not the Spirit of Christ--</hi>Again, this does not mean "the disposition or mind of Christ," but the Holy Ghost; here called "the Spirit of Christ," just as He is called "the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus" (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.8.2">Ro 8:2</reference>). It is as "the Spirit of Christ" that the Holy Ghost takes possession of believers, introducing into them all the gracious, dove-like disposition which dwelt in Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.16">Mt 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.34">Joh 3:34</reference>). Now if any man's heart be void, not of such dispositions, but of the blessed Author of them, "the Spirit of Christ."<div eID="gen32161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he is none of his--</hi>even though intellectually convinced of the truth of Christianity, and in a general sense influence by its spirit. Sharp, solemn statement this! <div eID="gen32162" type="x-p"/>
entries.37578f2d4dbaf014cc41de2809da021ee4c20395: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16507"/><div sID="gen32163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16507"/><hi type="bold">10-11. And if Christ be in you--</hi>by His indwelling Spirit in virtue of which we have one life with him.<div eID="gen32163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the body--</hi>"the body indeed."<div eID="gen32164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is dead because of--</hi>"by reason of"<div eID="gen32165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sin; but the spirit is life because--</hi>or, "by reason"<div eID="gen32166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of righteousness--</hi>The word "indeed," which the original requires, is of the nature of a concession--"I grant you that the body is dead ... and so far redemption is incomplete, but," &c.; that is, "If Christ be in you by His indwelling Spirit, though your 'bodies' have to pass through the stage of 'death' in consequence of the first Adam's 'sin,' your spirit is instinct with new and undying 'life,' brought in by the 'righteousness' of the second Adam" [Tholuck, Meyer, and Alford in part, but only Hodge entirely]. <div eID="gen32167" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9d77bb74afa2cc78998ef74fcf08fa387a08150: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16509"/><div sID="gen32174" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16509"/><hi type="bold">12-13. Therefore, brethren, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh--</hi>"Once we were sold under sin (<reference osisRef="Rom.7.14">Ro 7:14</reference>); but now that we have been set free from that hard master and become servants to Righteousness (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.22">Ro 6:22</reference>), we owe nothing to the flesh, we disown its unrighteous claims and are deaf to its imperious demands." Glorious sentiment! <div eID="gen32174" type="x-p"/>
entries.6a5a7606fb4f3fc5514f71757357055e8028fcbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16511"/><div sID="gen32180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16511"/><hi type="bold">14. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are the sons of God, they, &c.--</hi>"these are sons of God." Hitherto the apostle has spoken of the Spirit simply as a power through which believers mortify sin: now he speaks of Him as a gracious, loving Guide, whose "leading"--enjoyed by all in whom is the Spirit of God's dear Son--shows that they also are "sons of God." <div eID="gen32180" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fa6cc9fea04aab7a6b50f29dcbfb188e9c0c674: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16512"/><div sID="gen32181" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16512"/><hi type="bold">15. For, &c.--</hi>"For ye received not (at the time of your conversion) the spirit of bondage," that is, "The spirit ye received was not a spirit of bondage."<div eID="gen32181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">again--</hi>gendering.<div eID="gen32182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to fear--</hi>as under the law which "worketh wrath," that is, "Such was your condition before ye believed, living in legal bondage, haunted with incessant forebodings under a sense of unpardoned sin. But it was not to perpetuate that wretched state that ye received the Spirit."<div eID="gen32183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but ye have received--</hi>"ye received."<div eID="gen32184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spirit of adoption, whereby--</hi>rather, "wherein."<div eID="gen32185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32186" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we cry, Abba, Father--</hi>The word "cry" is emphatic, expressing the spontaneousness, the strength, and the exuberance of the final emotions. In <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Ga 4:6</reference> this cry is said to proceed from the Spirit in us, drawing forth the filial exclamation in our hearts. Here, it is said to proceed from our own hearts under the vitalizing energy of the Spirit, as the very element of the new life in believers (compare <reference osisRef="Matt.10.19">Mt 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">20</reference>; and see on <reference osisRef="Rom.8.4">Ro 8:4</reference>). "Abba" is the Syro-Chaldaic word for "Father"; and the Greek word for that is added, not surely to tell the reader that both mean the same thing, but for the same reason which drew both words from the lips of Christ Himself during his agony in the garden (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.36">Mr 14:36</reference>). He, doubtless, loved to utter His Father's name in both the accustomed forms; beginning with His cherished mother tongue, and adding that of the learned. In this view the use of both words here has a charming simplicity and warmth. <div eID="gen32186" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5422032410dc2aad548633bf598cb495ef79168: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16513"/><div sID="gen32187" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16513"/><hi type="bold">16. The Spirit itself--</hi>It should be "Himself" (see on <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Ro 8:26</reference>).<div eID="gen32187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32188" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children--</hi>"are children"<div eID="gen32188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of God--</hi>The testimony of our own spirit is borne in that cry of conscious sonship, "Abba, Father"; but we are not therein alone; for the Holy Ghost within us, yea, even in that very cry which it is His to draw forth, sets His own distinct seal to ours; and thus, "in the mouth of two witnesses" the thing is established. The apostle had before called us "sons of God," referring to our adoption; here the word changes to "children," referring to our new birth. The one expresses the dignity to which we are admitted; the other the new life which we receive. The latter is more suitable here; because a son by adoption might not be heir of the property, whereas a son by birth certainly is, and this is what the apostle is now coming to. <div eID="gen32189" type="x-p"/>
entries.1824807a3a71b830c5f458b2c71ce6528df00d02: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16514"/><div sID="gen32190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16514"/><hi type="bold">17. And if children, then heirs--</hi>"heirs also."<div eID="gen32190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heirs of God--</hi>of our Father's kingdom.<div eID="gen32191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32192" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and joint-heirs with Christ--</hi>as the "First-born among many brethren" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Ro 8:29</reference>), and as "Heir of all things" (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.2">He 1:2</reference>).<div eID="gen32192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32193" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if so be that we suffer--</hi>"provided we be suffering with Him."<div eID="gen32193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32194" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that we may be also glorified together--</hi>with Him. This necessity of conformity to Christ in suffering in order to participate in His glory, is taught alike by Christ Himself and by His apostles (<reference osisRef="John.12.24-John.12.26">Joh 12:24-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.16.24">Mt 16:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.25">25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">2Ti 2:12</reference>). <div eID="gen32194" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae6a2fdec0b6b2d96e080835f123d3e34c419b9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16515"/><div sID="gen32195" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16515"/><hi type="bold">18. For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us--</hi>that is, "True, we must suffer with Christ, if we would partake of His glory; but what of that? For if such sufferings are set over against the coming glory, they sink into insignificance." <div eID="gen32195" type="x-p"/>
entries.f12f1c3084052724800f40c3936a596c512bda6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16516"/><div sID="gen32196" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16516"/><hi type="bold">19-22. For, &c.--</hi>"The apostle, fired with the thought of the future glory of the saints, pours forth this splendid passage, in which he represents the whole creation groaning under its present degradation, and looking and longing for the revelation of this glory as the end and consummation of its existence" [Hodge].<div eID="gen32196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32197" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the earnest expectation--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Phil.1.20">Php 1:20</reference>).<div eID="gen32197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32198" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the creature--</hi>rather, "the creation."<div eID="gen32198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32199" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waiteth for the manifestation--</hi>"is waiting for the revelation"<div eID="gen32199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32200" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the sons of God--</hi>that is, "for the redemption of their bodies" from the grave (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.23">Ro 8:23</reference>), which will reveal their sonship, now hidden (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.20.36">Lu 20:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.7">Re 21:7</reference>). <div eID="gen32200" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d42e94d0777dff771ce3155f047cc78f91331b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16520"/><div sID="gen32210" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16520"/><hi type="bold">23. And not only they, but ourselves also--</hi>or "not only [so], but even we ourselves"--that is, besides the inanimate creation.<div eID="gen32210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32211" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which have the first-fruits of the Spirit--</hi>or, "the Spirit as the first-fruits" of our full redemption (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.22">2Co 1:22</reference>), moulding the heart to a heavenly frame and attempering it to its future element.<div eID="gen32211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32212" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">even we ourselves--</hi>though we have so much of heaven already within us.<div eID="gen32212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32213" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">groan within ourselves--</hi>under this "body of sin and death," and under the manifold "vanity and vexation of spirit" that are written upon every object and every pursuit and every enjoyment under the sun.<div eID="gen32213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32214" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">waiting for the--</hi>manifestation of our<div eID="gen32214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32215" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body--</hi>from the grave: "not (be it observed) the deliverance of ourselves from the body, but the redemption of the body itself from the grave" [Bengel]. <div eID="gen32215" type="x-p"/>
entries.227ba51ae190df46af738dfd98b0ca26c12faabe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16521"/><div sID="gen32216" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16521"/><hi type="bold">24. For we are saved by hope--</hi>rather, "For in hope we are saved"; that is, it is more a salvation in hope than as yet in actual possession.<div eID="gen32216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32217" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but hope that is seen is not hope--</hi>for the very meaning of hope is, the expectation that something now future will become present.<div eID="gen32217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32218" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?--</hi>the latter ending when the other comes. <div eID="gen32218" type="x-p"/>
entries.af575a08b116d1201574e6a0104ff34cc79ba339: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16522"/><div sID="gen32219" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16522"/><hi type="bold">25. But if we hope for that we see not, then do we with patience wait for it--</hi>that is, then, patient waiting for it is our fitting attitude. <div eID="gen32219" type="x-p"/>
entries.40ea7ff0f12bb72df6525dd7fef8fb693eb40aec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16523"/><div sID="gen32220" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16523"/><hi type="bold">26-27. Likewise the Spirit also, &c.--</hi>or, "But after the like manner doth the Spirit also help.<div eID="gen32220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32221" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">our infirmities--</hi>rather (according to the true reading), "our infirmity"; not merely the one infirmity here specified, but the general weakness of the spiritual life in its present state, of which one example is here given.<div eID="gen32221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32222" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for we know not what we should pray for as we ought--</hi>It is not the proper matter of prayer that believers are at so much loss about, for the fullest directions are given them on this head: but to ask for the right things "as they ought" is the difficulty. This arises partly from the dimness of our spiritual vision in the present veiled state, while we have to "walk by faith, not by sight" (see on <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.9">1Co 13:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.7">2Co 5:7</reference>), and the large admixture of the ideas and feelings which spring from the fleeting objects of sense that there is in the very best views and affections of our renewed nature; partly also from the necessary imperfection of all human language as a vehicle for expressing the subtle spiritual feelings of the heart. In these circumstances, how can it be but that much uncertainty should surround all our spiritual exercises, and that in our nearest approaches and in the freest outpourings of our hearts to our Father in heaven, doubts should spring up within us whether our frame of mind in such exercises is altogether befitting and well pleasing to God? Nor do these anxieties subside, but rather deepen, with the depth and ripeness of our spiritual experience.<div eID="gen32222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32223" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but the Spirit itself--</hi>rather, "Himself." (See end of <reference osisRef="Rom.8.27">Ro 8:27</reference>).<div eID="gen32223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32224" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered--</hi>that is, which cannot be expressed in articulate language. Sublime and affecting ideas, for which we are indebted to this passage alone! "As we struggle to express in articulate language the desires of our hearts and find that our deepest emotions are the most inexpressible, we 'groan' under this felt inability. But not in vain are these groanings. For 'the Spirit Himself' is in them, giving to the emotions which He Himself has kindled the only language of which they are capable; so that though on our part they are the fruit of impotence to utter what we feel, they are at the same time the intercession of the Spirit Himself in our behalf." <div eID="gen32224" type="x-p"/>
entries.7e4cbe78a2796f6aa015d72858e7f40a897fde44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16525"/><div sID="gen32230" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16525"/><hi type="bold">28. And--</hi>or, "Moreover," or "Now"; noting a transition to a new particular.<div eID="gen32230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32231" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we know, &c.--</hi>The order in the original is more striking: "We know that to them that love God" (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1Co 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.24">Ep 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.12">Jas 1:12</reference>; 2:5) "all things work together for good [even] to them who are the called (rather, 'who are called') according to His (eternal) purpose." Glorious assurance! And this, it seems, was a "household word," a "known" thing, among believers. This working of all things for good is done quite naturally to "them that love God," because such souls, persuaded that He who gave His own Son for them cannot but mean them well in all His procedure, learn thus to take in good part whatever He sends them, however trying to flesh and blood: and to them who are the called, according to "His purpose," all things do in the same intelligible way "work together for good"; for, even when "He hath His way in the whirlwind," they see "His chariot paved with love" (<reference osisRef="Song.3.10">So 3:10</reference>). And knowing that it is in pursuance of an eternal "purpose" of love that they have been "called into the fellowship of His Son Jesus Christ" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">1Co 1:9</reference>), they naturally say within themselves, "It cannot be that He 'of whom, and through whom, and to whom are all things,' should suffer that purpose to be thwarted by anything really adverse to us, or that He should not make all things, dark as well as light, crooked as well as straight, to co-operate to the furtherance and final completion of His high design." <div eID="gen32231" type="x-p"/>
entries.3bb4d1585874bb880b278ca2b8231207b2add048: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16526"/><div sID="gen32232" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16526"/><hi type="bold">29. For--</hi>as touching this "calling according to his purpose" (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Ro 8:28</reference>).<div eID="gen32232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32233" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom he did foreknow he also did predestinate--</hi>foreordain. In what sense are we to take the word "foreknow" here? "Those who He foreknew would repent and believe," say Pelagians of every age and every hue. But this is to thrust into the text what is contrary to the whole spirit, and even letter, of the apostle's teaching (see <reference osisRef="Rom.9.11">Ro 9:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Rom.11.2">Ro 11:2</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>, God's "knowledge" of His people cannot be restricted to a mere foresight of future events, or acquaintance with what is passing here below. Does "whom He did foreknow," then, mean "whom He foreordained?" Scarcely, because both "foreknowledge" and "foreordination" are here mentioned, and the one as the cause of the other. It is difficult indeed for our limited minds to distinguish them as states of the Divine Mind towards men; especially since in <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Ac 2:23</reference> "the counsel" is put before "the foreknowledge of God," while in <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.2">1Pe 1:2</reference> "election" is said to be "according to the foreknowledge of God." But probably God's foreknowledge of His own people means His "peculiar, gracious, complacency in them," while His "predestinating" or "foreordaining" them signifies His fixed purpose, flowing from this, to "save them and call them with an holy calling" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen32233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32234" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be conformed to the image of his Son--</hi>that is, to be His sons after the pattern, model, or image of His Sonship in our nature.<div eID="gen32234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32235" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that he might be the first-born among many brethren--</hi>"The First-born," the Son by nature; His "many brethren," sons by adoption: He, in the Humanity of the Only-begotten of the Father, bearing our sins on the accursed tree; they in that of mere men ready to perish by reason of sin, but redeemed by His blood from condemnation and wrath, and transformed into His likeness: He "the First-born from the dead"; they "that sleep in Jesus," to be in due time "brought with Him"; "The First-born," now "crowned with glory and honor"; His "many brethren," "when He shall appear, to be like Him, for they shall see Him as He is." <div eID="gen32235" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c1abab4f24cc8dbabf262d56bc895a698dcde83: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16527"/><div sID="gen32236" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16527"/><hi type="bold">30. Moreover--</hi>"And," or "Now"; explanatory of <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Ro 8:29</reference>--In "predestinating us to be conformed to the image of His Son" in final glory, He settled all the successive steps of it. Thus<div eID="gen32236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32237" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whom he did predestinate, them he also called--</hi>The word "called" (as Hodge and others truly observe) is never in the Epistles of the New Testament applied to those who have only the outward invitation of the Gospel (as in <reference osisRef="Matt.20.16">Mt 20:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.14">22:14</reference>). It always means "internally, effectually, savingly called." It denotes the first great step in personal salvation and answers to "conversion." Only the word conversion expresses the change of character which then takes place, whereas this "calling" expresses the divine authorship of the change, and the sovereign power by which we are summoned, Matthew-like, Zaccheus-like, out of our old, wretched, perishing condition, into a new, safe, blessed life.<div eID="gen32237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32238" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and whom he called--</hi>thus.<div eID="gen32238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32239" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">them he also justified--</hi>brought into the definite state of reconciliation already so fully described.<div eID="gen32239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32240" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and whom he justified, them he also glorified--</hi>brought to final glory (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.17">Ro 8:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.18">18</reference>). Noble climax, and so rhythmically expressed! And all this is viewed as past; because, starting from the past decree of "predestination to be conformed to the image of God's Son" of which the other steps are but the successive unfoldings--all is beheld as one entire, eternally completed salvation. <div eID="gen32240" type="x-p"/>
entries.03edb4f0c255ea48da4b7053500ae94392e72e60: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16528"/><div sID="gen32241" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16528"/><hi type="bold">31. What shall we then say to these things?--</hi>"We can no farther go, think, wish" [Bengel]. This whole passage, to <reference osisRef="Rom.8.34">Ro 8:34</reference>, and even to the end of the chapter, strikes all thoughtful interpreters and readers, as transcending almost every thing in language, while Olshausen notices the "profound and colossal" character of the thought.<div eID="gen32241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32242" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">If God be for us, who can be against us?--</hi>If God be resolved and engaged to bring us through, all our enemies must be His; and "Who would set the briers and thorns against Him in battle? He would go through them. He would burn them together" (<reference osisRef="Isa.27.4">Is 27:4</reference>). What strong consolation is here! Nay, but the great Pledge of all has already been given; for, <div eID="gen32242" type="x-p"/>
entries.5788c237ffb11fde69aac6b6d51363c72f18723f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16529"/><div sID="gen32243" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16529"/><hi type="bold">32. He--</hi>rather, "He surely." (It is a pity to lose the emphatic particle of the original).<div eID="gen32243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32244" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that spared not--</hi>"withheld not," "kept not back." This expressive phrase, as well as the whole thought, is suggested by <reference osisRef="Gen.22.12">Ge 22:12</reference>, where Jehovah's touching commendation of Abraham's conduct regarding his son Isaac seems designed to furnish something like a glimpse into the spirit of His own act in surrendering His own Son. "Take now (said the Lord to Abraham) thy son, thine only, whom thou lovest, and ... offer him for a burnt offering" (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.2">Ge 22:2</reference>); and only when Abraham had all but performed that loftiest act of self-sacrifice, the Lord interposed, saying, "Now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou HAST NOT WITHHELD THY SON, THINE ONLY SON, from Me." In the light of this incident, then, and of this language, our apostle can mean to convey nothing less than this, that in "not sparing His own Son, but delivering Him up," or surrendering Him, God exercised, in His Paternal character, a mysterious act of Self-sacrifice, which, though involving none of the pain and none of the loss which are inseparable from the very idea of self-sacrifice on our part, was not less real, but, on the contrary, as far transcended any such acts of ours as His nature is above the creature's. But this is inconceivable if Christ be not God's "own (or proper) Son," partaker of His very nature, as really as Isaac was of his father Abraham's. In that sense, certainly, the Jews charged our Lord with making Himself "equal with God" (see on <reference osisRef="John.5.18">Joh 5:18</reference>), which He in reply forthwith proceeded, not to disown, but to illustrate and confirm. Understand Christ's Sonship thus, and the language of Scripture regarding it is intelligible and harmonious; but take it to be an artificial relationship, ascribed to Him in virtue either of His miraculous birth, or His resurrection from the dead, or the grandeur of His works, or all of these together--and the passages which speak of it neither explain of themselves nor harmonize with each other.<div eID="gen32244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32245" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">delivered him up--</hi>not to death merely (as many take it), for that is too narrow an idea here, but "surrendered Him" in the most comprehensive sense; compare <reference osisRef="John.3.16">Joh 3:16</reference>, "God so loved the world that He GAVE His only-begotten Son."<div eID="gen32245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32246" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for us all--</hi>that is, for all believers alike; as nearly every good interpreter admits must be the meaning here.<div eID="gen32246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32247" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how shall he not--</hi>how can we conceive that He should not.<div eID="gen32247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32248" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with him also--</hi>rather, "also with Him." (The word "also" is often so placed in our version as to obscure the sense; see on <reference osisRef="Heb.12.1">He 12:1</reference>).<div eID="gen32248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32249" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">freely give us all things?--</hi>all other gifts being not only immeasurably less than this Gift of gifts, but virtually included in it. <div eID="gen32249" type="x-p"/>
entries.37d6191af83942081050da29ac7a60d703dadd70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16530"/><div sID="gen32250" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16530"/><hi type="bold">33-34. Who shall lay anything to the charge of--</hi>or, "bring any charge against."<div eID="gen32250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32251" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God's elect?--</hi>the first place in this Epistle where believers are styled "the elect." In what sense this is meant will appear in next chapter. <div eID="gen32251" type="x-p"/>
entries.87cd6788066e9f94e342e33083442b1584c409b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16532"/><div sID="gen32256" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16532"/><hi type="bold">35-36. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?--</hi>This does not mean "our love to Christ," as if, Who shall hinder us from loving Christ? but "Christ's love to us," as is clear from the closing words of the chapter, which refer to the same subject. Nor would the other sense harmonize with the scope of the chapter, which is to exhibit the ample ground of the believer's confidence in Christ. "It is no ground of confidence to assert, or even to feel, that we will never forsake Christ; but it is the strongest ground of assurance to be convinced that His love will never change" [Hodge].<div eID="gen32256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32257" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall tribulation, &c.--</hi>"None of these, nor all together, how terrible soever to the flesh, are tokens of God's wrath, or the least ground for doubt of His love. From whom could such a question come better than from one who had himself for Christ's sake endured so much? (See <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.11-2Cor.11.33">2Co 11:11-33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.10-1Cor.4.13">1Co 4:10-13</reference>). The apostle says not (remarks Calvin nobly) "What," but "Who," just as if all creatures and all afflictions were so many gladiators taking arms against the Christians [Tholuck]. <div eID="gen32257" type="x-p"/>
entries.139f3f56f5da6a7514a1fff5560835ca1f168fcb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16534"/><div sID="gen32259" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16534"/><hi type="bold">37. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors, through him that loved us--</hi>not, "We are so far from being conquered by them, that they do us much good" [Hodge]; for though this be true, the word means simply, "We are pre-eminently conquerors." See on <reference osisRef="Rom.5.20">Ro 5:20</reference>. And so far are they from "separating us from Christ's love," that it is just "through Him that loved us" that we are victorious over them. <div eID="gen32259" type="x-p"/>
entries.60187c2c937ea744974d6681c24ac580474638cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16535"/><div sID="gen32260" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16535"/><hi type="bold">38-39. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers--</hi>whether good or bad. But as the bad are not called "angels," or "principalities," or "powers," save with some addition to show that such are meant (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.41">Mt 25:41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.15">Col 2:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.6.12">Ep 6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2Pe 2:4</reference>--except perhaps <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.3">1Co 6:3</reference>), probably the good are meant here, but merely as the same apostle supposes an angel from heaven to preach a false gospel. (So the best interpreters).<div eID="gen32260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32261" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor things present, nor things to come--</hi>no condition of the present life and none of the unknown possibilities of the life to come. <div eID="gen32261" type="x-p"/>

entries.caa3f6e4bc82070b6c0e2c6050066a6b83f682f9: <div eID="gen46502" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen46503" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46504" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46504" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen46503" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen46505" type="x-p"/> The happy state of those who believe in Christ, and walk under the influence of his Spirit, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.1">Rom 8:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.2">Rom 8:2</reference>. The design of God in sending his Son into the world was to redeem men from sin, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.3">Rom 8:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.4">Rom 8:4</reference>. The miserable state of the carnally minded, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.6-Rom.8.8">Rom 8:6-8</reference>. How Christ lives and works in his followers; their blessedness here, and their happiness hereafter, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.9-Rom.8.17">Rom 8:9-17</reference>. Sufferings are the common lot of all men; and from which Gentiles and Jews have the hope of being finally delivered, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.18-Rom.8.23">Rom 8:18-23</reference>. The use and importance of hope, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.24">Rom 8:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.25">Rom 8:25</reference>. The Spirit makes intercession for the followers of Christ, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Rom 8:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.27">Rom 8:27</reference>. All things work together for good to them that love God, and who act according to his gracious purpose in calling them, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Rom 8:28</reference>. The means used to bring men to eternal glory, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.29">Rom 8:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.30">Rom 8:30</reference>. The great blessedness, confidence, and security of all genuine Christians, whom, while they hold fast faith and a good conscience, nothing can separate from the love of God, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.31-Rom.8.39">Rom 8:31-39</reference>. <div eID="gen46505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46506" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen46506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46507" type="x-p"/> There is, therefore, now no condemnation - To do justice to St. Paul's reasoning, this chapter must be read in the closest connection with the preceding. There we have seen the unavailing struggles of an awakened Jew, who sought pardon and holiness from that law which he was conscious he had broken; and in which he could find no provision for pardon, and no power to sanctify. This conviction having brought him to the very brink of despair, and, being on the point of giving up all hope, he hears of redemption by Jesus Christ, thanks God for the prospect he has of salvation, applies for and receives it; and now magnifies God for the unspeakable gift of which he has been made a partaker. <div eID="gen46507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46508" type="x-p"/> Those who restrain the word now, so as to indicate by it the Gospel dispensation only, do not take in the whole of the apostles meaning. The apostle has not been dealing in general matters only, but also in those which are particular. He has not been pointing out merely the difference between the two dispensations, the Mosaic and the Christian; but he marks out the state of a penitent under the former, and that of a believer under the latter. The last chapter closed with an account of the deep distress of the penitent; this one opens with an account of his salvation. The now, therefore, in the text, must refer more to the happy transition from darkness to light, from condemnation to pardon, which this believer now enjoys, than to the Christian dispensation taking the place of the Jewish economy. <div eID="gen46508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46509" type="x-p"/> Who walk not after the flesh, etc. - In this one verse we find the power and virtue of the Gospel scheme; it pardons and sanctifies; the Jewish law could do neither. By faith in our Lord Jesus Christ the penitent, condemned by the law, is pardoned; the carnal man, labouring under the overpowering influence of the sin of his nature, is sanctified. He is first freely justified; he feels no condemnation; he is fully sanctified; he walks not after the Flesh, but after the Spirit. <div eID="gen46509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46510" type="x-p"/> This last clause is wanting in the principal MSS., versions, and fathers. Griesbach has excluded it from the text; and Dr. White says, Certissime delenda; it should most undoubtedly be expunged. Without it, the passage reads thus: There is, therefore, no condemnation to them that are in Christ Jesus; for the law of the Spirit of life, etc. It is a fairly assumed point, that those who are in Christ Jesus, who believe in his name, have redemption in his blood; are made partakers of his Spirit, and have the mind in them that was in him; will not walk after the flesh, but after the Spirit: therefore the thing itself is included in the being in Christ, whether it be expressed or not: and it was probably to make the thing more obvious, that this explanatory clause was added by some copyist, for it does not appear to have made an original part of the text; and it is most likely that it was inserted here from the fourth verse.
entries.ad5b2a1e1217ea035a017076ff4da6debdf478bd: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen46510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46511" type="x-p"/> For the law of the Spirit of life - The Gospel of the grace of Christ, which is not only a law or rule of life, but affords that sovereign energy by which guilt is removed from the conscience, the power of sin broken, and its polluting influence removed from the heart. The law was a spirit of death, by which those who were under it were bound down, because of their sin, to condemnation and death. The Gospel proclaims Jesus the Savior; and what the law bound unto death, It looses unto life eternal. And thus the apostle says, whether of himself or the man whom he is still personating, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death. Most people allow that St. Paul is here speaking of his own state; and this state is so totally different from that described in the preceding chapter, that it is absolutely impossible that they should have been the state of the same being, at one and the same time. No creature could possibly be carnal, sold under sin, brought into captivity to the law of sin and death; and at the same time be made free from that law of sin and death, by the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus! Until the most palpable absurdities and contradictions can be reconciled, these two opposite states can never exist in the same person at the same time.
entries.e8c7087cb047ff8ffdc0f174b666ed3f66989f67: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen46511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46512" type="x-p"/> For what the law could not do - The law could not pardon; the law could not sanctify; the law could not dispense with its own requisitions; it is the rule of righteousness, and therefore must condemn unrighteousness. This is its unalterable nature. Had there been perfect obedience to its dictates, instead of condemning, it would have applauded and rewarded; but as the flesh, the carnal and rebellious principle, had prevailed, and transgression had taken place, it was rendered weak, inefficient to undo this word of the flesh, and bring the sinner into a state of pardon and acceptance with God. <div eID="gen46512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46513" type="x-p"/> God sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh - Did that which the law could not do; i.e. purchased pardon for the sinner, and brought every believer into the favor of God. And this is effected by the incarnation of Christ: He, in whom dwelt the fullness of the Godhead bodily, took upon him the likeness of sinful flesh, that is, a human body like ours, but not sinful as ours; and for sin, και περι ἁμαρτιας, and as a Sacrifice for Sin, (this is the sense of the word in a multitude of places), condemned sin in the flesh - condemned that to death and destruction which had condemned us to both. <div eID="gen46513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46514" type="x-p"/> Condemned sin in the flesh - The design and object of the incarnation and sacrifice of Christ was to condemn sin, to have it executed and destroyed; not to tolerate it as some think, or to render it subservient to the purposes of his grace, as others; but to annihilate its power, guilt, and being in the soul of a believer.
entries.a5f0568c10f71c0041f0c8110b8bb7a7ede3d4c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen46514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46515" type="x-p"/> That the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us - That the guilt might be pardoned through the merit of that sacrifice; and that we might be enabled, by the power of his own grace and Spirit, to walk in newness of life; loving God with all our heart, soul, mind, and strength, and our neighbor as ourselves: and thus the righteousness, the spirit, design, and purpose of the law is fulfilled in us, through the strength of the Spirit of Christ, which is here put in opposition to the weakness of the law through the flesh. <div eID="gen46515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46516" type="x-p"/> It is very likely that the concluding clause of this verse, which is the very same as that found in the common text of the first verse, has been transferred to that verse from this place.
entries.3831119acd3cb2fe93ddcecce5a2521e55078bab: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen46516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46517" type="x-p"/> For they that are after the flesh - And here is the great distinction between Jews and genuine Christians: the former are after the flesh - are under the power of the carnal, rebellious principle; and consequently mind, προνουσιν, relish, the things of the flesh - the things which appertain merely to the present life; having no relish for spiritual and eternal things. <div eID="gen46517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46518" type="x-p"/> But they that are after the Spirit - They who are regenerated, who are born of the Spirit, being redeemed from the influence and law of the carnal mind; these relish the things of the Spirit - they are spiritually minded, and pass through things temporal, so as not to lose the things which are eternal. And this, which in these apostolic times distinguished between the carnal Jew and the spiritual believer in Christ, is the grand mark of distinction between the nominal and the real Christian now. The former is earthly minded, and lives for this world; the latter is spiritually minded, and lives for the world to come.
entries.7246786d8d111f86852bb4ea2f7987fb5cb96ea7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen46518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46519" type="x-p"/> For to be carnally minded is death - To live under the influence of the carnal mind is to live in the state of condemnation, and consequently liable to death eternal: whereas, on the contrary, he who is spiritually minded has the life and peace of God in his soul, and is in full prospect of life eternal.
entries.5f8e520e7eb5e1ce8719936521e21ef7295386da: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen46519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46520" type="x-p"/> Because the carnal mind is enmity against God - Because it is a carnal mind, and relishes earthly and sinful things, and lives in opposition to the pure and holy law of God: therefore, it is enmity against God; it is irreconcilable and implacable hatred. <div eID="gen46520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46521" type="x-p"/> It is not subject to the law of God - It will come under no obedience; for it is sin, and the very principle of rebellion; and therefore it cannot be subject, nor subjected; for it is essential to sin to show itself in rebellion; and when it ceases to rebel, it ceases to be sin. <div eID="gen46521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46522" type="x-p"/> From this we learn that the design of God in the economy of the Gospel, is not to weaken, curtail, or lay the carnal principle in bonds, but to destroy it. As it is not subject, and cannot be subject, to the law of God, it must be destroyed, else it will continue to rebel against God. It cannot be mended, or rendered less offensive in its nature, even by the operations of God; it is ever sin, and sin is ever enmity; and enmity, wherever it has power, will invariably show itself in acts of hostility and rebellion.
entries.9619ce659ac3481259e45c2809a896110f9b4d4b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen46522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46523" type="x-p"/> So then - Because this carnal mind is enmity against God, they that are in the flesh - who are under the power of the workings of this carnal mind, (which every soul is that has not received redemption in the blood of the Lamb), - <div eID="gen46523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46524" type="x-p"/> Cannot please God - Because of the rebellious workings of this principle of rebellion and hatred. And, if they cannot please God, they must be displeasing to him; and consequently in the broad road to final perdition.
entries.9c07ccbb546b5e4b4864edfcc65d9f5b462417c3: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen46524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46525" type="x-p"/> But ye are not in the flesh - Ye Christians, who have believed in Christ Jesus as the sin offering which has condemned sin in the flesh; and, having been justified by faith and made partakers of the Holy Spirit, are enabled to walk in newness of life. <div eID="gen46525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46526" type="x-p"/> If so be that the Spirit of God dwell in you - Or seeing that, ειπερ, the Spirit of God dwelleth in you. The flesh, the sinful principle, dwelt in them before; and its motions were the proofs of its indwelling; but now the Spirit dwells in them; and its testimony in their conscience, and its powerful operations in their hearts, are the proofs of its indwelling. God made man in union with himself, and his heart was his temple. Sin being committed, the temple was defiled, and God abandoned it. Jesus Christ is come by his sacrifice and Spirit to cleanse the temple, and make man again a habitation of God through the Spirit. And when this almighty Spirit again makes the heart his residence, then the soul is delivered from the moral effects of the fall. And that this is absolutely necessary to our present peace and final salvation is proved from this: that if any man have not the Spirit of Christ - the mind that was in him, produced there by the power of the Holy Ghost - he is none of his; he does not belong to the kingdom, flock, or family of God. This is an awful conclusion! Reader, lay it to heart.
entries.63f9271bc8c57e9478b5e64da3cd2ea8ae463a03: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen46526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen46527" type="x-p"/> And if Christ be in you, etc. - This is the criterion by which you may judge of the state of grace in which ye stand. If Christ dwell in your hearts by faith, the body is dead because of sin, δι' ἁμαρτιαν, in reference to sin; the members of your body no more perform the work of sin than the body of a dead man does the functions of natural life.
