He does not, however, mean, that nothing shall oppose us; but he promises a victory over all kinds of enemies.<div eID="gen114574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114575" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">If God be for us</hi>, <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> This is the chief and the only support which can sustain us in every temptation. For except we have God propitious to us, though all things should smile on us, yet no sure confidence can be attained: but, on the other hand, his favor alone is a sufficient solace in every sorrow, a protection sufficiently strong against all the storms of adversities. And on this subject there are many testimonies of Scripture, which show that when the saints rely on the power of God alone, they dare to despise whatever is opposed to them in the world.<div eID="gen114575" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114576" type="x-p"/>“When I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall not fear evils, for thou art with me.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.23.4">Psalm 23:4</reference>.)<div eID="gen114576" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114577" type="x-p"/>“In the Lord I trust: what shall flesh do to me.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.56.11">Psalm 56:11</reference>.)<div eID="gen114577" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114578" type="x-p"/>“I shall not fear the thousands of the people who beset me.”<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.3.6">Psalm 3:6</reference>.)<div eID="gen114578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114579" type="x-p"/>For there is no power either under or above the heavens, which can resist the arm of God. Having him then as our defender, we need fear no harm whatever. Hence he alone shows real confidence in God, who being content with his protection, dreads nothing in such a way as to despond; the faithful are doubtless often shaken but are never utterly cast down. In short, the Apostle’s object was to show, that the godly soul ought to rely on the inward testimony of the Holy Spirit, and not to depend on outward things.<div eID="gen114579" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114573" osisID="Rom.8.31" type="section"/>
entries.c6a605d4bd67ee1e26fc593f20ad1fb5aad4f275: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.32" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.8.32" sID="gen114580" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114581" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">32.</hi> <hi type="italic">He who has not spared his own son,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> As it greatly concerns us to be so thoroughly persuaded of the paternal love of God, as to be able to retain our rejoicing on its account, Paul brings forward the price of our redemption in order to prove that God favors us: and doubtless it is a remarkable and clear evidence of inappreciable love, that the Father refused not to bestow his Son for our salvation. And so Paul draws an argument from the greater to the less, that as he had nothing dearer, or more precious, or more excellent than his Son, he will neglect nothing of what he foresees will be profitable to us. <note n="273"> <div sID="gen114582" type="x-p"/> <name>Calvin</name> renders χαρίσεται by “<foreign xml:lang="la">donaret</foreign>;” <name>Capellus</name> more fully, “<foreign xml:lang="la">gratis donabit</foreign> — will gratuitously give.” Christ himself, and everything that comes with or through him, is a favor freely bestowed, and not what we merit. This shuts out, as <name>Pareus</name> observes, everything as meritorious on the part of man. All is grace. The “all things” include every thing necessary for salvation — every grace now and eternal glory hereafter. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114582" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen114581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114583" type="x-p"/>This passage ought to remind us of what Christ brings to us, and to awaken us to contemplate his riches; for as he is a pledge of God’s infinite love towards us, so he has not been sent to us void of blessings or empty, but filled with all celestial treasures, so that they who possess him may not want anything necessary for their perfect felicity. To <hi type="italic">deliver up</hi> means here to expose to death.<div eID="gen114583" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.32" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114580" osisID="Rom.8.32" type="section"/>
entries.a5b91abe5d31e1c54079b9a08ac26caf9762c752: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.33" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.8.33" sID="gen114584" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114585" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">33.</hi> <hi type="italic">Who shall bring an accusation,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> The first and the chief consolation of the godly in adversities, is to be fully persuaded of the paternal kindness of God; for hence arises the certainty of their salvation, and that calm quietness of the soul through which it comes that adversities are sweetened, or at least the bitterness of sorrow mitigated. Hardly then a more suitable encouragement to patience could be adduced than this, a conviction that God is propitious to us; and hence Paul makes this confidence the main ground of that consolation, by which it behoves the faithful to be strengthened against all evils. And as the salvation of man is first assailed by accusation, and then subverted by condemnation, he in the first place averts the danger of accusation. There is indeed but one God, at whose tribunal we must stand; then there is no room for accusation when he justifies us. The antithetic clauses seem not indeed to be exactly arranged; for the two parts which ought rather to have been set in opposition to each other are these: “Who shall accuse? Christ is he who intercedes:” and then these two might have been connected, “Who shall condemn? God is he who justifies;” for God’s absolution answers to condemnation, and Christ’s intercession to accusation. But Paul has not without reason made another arrangement, as he was anxious to arm the children of God, as they say, from head to foot, with that confidence which banishes all anxieties and fears. He then more emphatically concludes, that the children of God are not subject to an accusation, because God justifies, than if he had said that Christ is our advocate; for he more fully expresses that the way to a trial is more completely closed up when the judge himself pronounces him wholly exempt from guilt, whom the accuser would bring in as deserving of punishment. There is also a similar reason for the second clause; for he shows that the faithful are very far from being involved in the danger of condemnation, since Christ by expiating their sins has anticipated the judgment of God, and by his intercession not only abolishes death, but also covers our sins in oblivion, so that they come not to an account.<div eID="gen114585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114586" type="x-p"/>The drift of the whole is, that we are not only freed from terror by present remedies, but that God comes to our aid beforehand, that he may better provide for our confidence.<div eID="gen114586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114587" type="x-p"/>But it must be here observed, as we have before reminded you, that to be justified, according to Paul, is to be absolved by the sentence of God, and to be counted just; and it is not difficult to prove this from the present passage, in which he reasons by affirming one thing which nullifies its opposite; for to absolve and to regard persons as guilty, are contrary things. Hence God will allow no accusation against us, because he has absolved us from all sins. The devil no doubt is an accuser of all the godly: the very law of God and their own conscience convict them; but all these prevail nothing with the judge, who justifies them. Therefore no adversary can shake or endanger our salvation.<div eID="gen114587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114588" type="x-p"/>Further, he so mentions the elect, as one who doubted not but that he was of their number; and he knew this, not by special revelation, (as some sophists falsely imagine,) but by a perception (<foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">sensu</hi></foreign> - feeling) common to all the godly. What then is here said of the elect, every one of the godly, according to the example of Paul, may apply to himself; for this doctrine would have been not only frigid, but wholly lifeless had he buried election in the secret purpose of God. But when we know, that there is here designedly set before us what every one of the godly ought to appropriate to himself, there is no doubt but that we are all encouraged to examine our calling, so that we may become assured that we are the children of God.<div eID="gen114588" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.33" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114584" osisID="Rom.8.33" type="section"/>
entries.043c4c36c534372236f0f0e54ef8359c3ed8f140:
34. Who is he that condemns? etc. As no one by accusing can prevail, when the judge absolves; so there remains no condemnation, when satisfaction is given to the laws, and the penalty is already paid. Now Christ is he, who, having once for all suffered the punishment due to us, thereby declared that he undertook our cause, in order to deliver us: he then who seeks hereafter to condemn us, must bring back Christ himself to death again. But he has not only died, but also came forth, by a resurrection, as the conqueror of death and triumphed over all its power.
He adds still more, — that he now sits at the right hand of the Father; by which is meant, that he possesses dominion over heaven and earth, and full power and rule over all things, according to what is said in Ephesians 1:20. He teaches us also, that he thus sits, that he may be a perpetual advocate and intercessor in securing our salvation. It hence follows, that when any one seeks to condemn us, he not only seeks to render void the death of Christ, but also contends with that unequalled power with which the Father has honored him, and who with that power conferred on him supreme authority. This so great an assurance; which dares to triumph over the devil, death, sin, and the gates of hell, ought to lodge deep in the hearts of all the godly; for our faith is nothing, except we feel assured that Christ is ours, and that the Father is in him propitious to us. Nothing then can be devised more pestilent and ruinous, than the scholastic dogma respecting the uncertainty of salvation.
Who intercedes, etc. It was necessary expressly to add this, lest the Divine majesty of Christ should terrify us. Though, then, from his elevated throne he holds all things in subjection under his feet, yet Paul represents him as a Mediator; whose presence it would be strange for us to dread, since he not only kindly invites us to himself, but also appears an intercessor for us before the Father. But we must not measure this intercession by our carnal judgment; for we must not suppose that he humbly supplicates the Father with bended knees and expanded hands; but as he appears continually, as one who died and rose again, and as his death and resurrection stand in the place of eternal intercession, and have the efficacy of a powerful prayer for reconciling and rendering the Father propitious to us, he is justly said to intercede for us.
Romans 8:35-37
35. Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?
35. Quis nos dirimet
“Dirimet — break us off,” divide or part us; χωρίσει — set apart, sever, separate: τίς, “who,” may be rendered, “what,” as מי in Hebrew. It is not put, it may be, in the neuter gender, because of the gender of the nouns which follow. As the Hebrews use often the future for the potential mood, so the case may be here — “What can separate us from the love of Christ? tribulation, or distress?” etc. It ought also to be added, that the verb “separate,” is used to designate divorce or separation between man and his wife. See Matthew 19:6; 1 Corinthians 7:10, 11, 15. — Ed.
a dilectione Christi? tribulatio, an angustia, an persequutio, an fames, an nuditas, an periculum, an gladius?
36. As it is written, For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.
36. Quemadmodum scriptum est, Quod propter te morimur quotidie, reputati sumus tanquam oves mactationi destinatæ:
37. Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.
37. Sed in iis omnibus supervincimus per eum qui dilexit nos.
entries.cb0092f08f66438c8b274b76c61502d797282052: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.35" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.8.35" sID="gen114602" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114603" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">35.</hi> <hi type="italic">Who shall separate us</hi>, <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> The conviction of safety is now more widely extended, even to lower things; for he who is persuaded of God’s kindness towards him, is able to stand firm in the heaviest afflictions. These usually harass men in no small degree, and for various reasons, — because they interpret them as tokens of God’s wrath, or think themselves to be forsaken by God, or see no end to them, or neglect to meditate on a better life, or for other similar reasons; but when the mind is purged from such mistakes, it becomes calm, and quietly rests. But the import of the words is, — That whatever happens, we ought to stand firm in this faith, — that God, who once in his love embraced us, never ceases to care for us. For he does not simply say that there is nothing which can tear God away from his love to us; but he means, that the knowledge and lively sense of the love which he testifies to us is so vigorous in our hearts, that it always shines in the darkness of afflictions: for as clouds, though they obscure the clear brightness of the sun, do not yet wholly deprive us of its light; so God, in adversities, sends forth through the darkness the rays of his favor, lest temptations should overwhelm us with despair; nay, our faith, supported by God’s promises as by wings, makes its way upward to heaven through all the intervening obstacles. It is indeed true, that adversities are tokens of God’s wrath, when viewed in themselves; but when pardon and reconciliation precede, we ought to be assured that God, though he chastises us, yet never forgets his mercy: he indeed thus reminds us of what we have deserved; but he no less testifies, that our salvation is an object of his care, while he leads us to repentance.<div eID="gen114603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114604" type="x-p"/>But he calls it<hi type="italic"> the love of Christ</hi>, and for this reason, — because the Father has in a manner opened his compassions to us in him. As then the love of God is not to be sought out of Christ, Paul rightly directs to him our attention, so that our faith may behold, in the rays of Christ’s favor, the serene countenance of the Father. The meaning is, — that in no adversities ought our confidence to be shaken as to this truth — that when God is propitious, nothing can be adverse to us. Some take this love in a passive sense, for that by which he is loved by us, as though Paul would have us armed with invincible courage <note n="275"> <div sID="gen114605" type="x-p"/> According to <name>Poole</name>, several of the Fathers entertained this opinion, such as <name>Origen</name>, <name>Chrysostom</name>, <name>Theodoret</name>, and <name>Ambrose</name><hi type="italic">:</hi> but even <name>Hammond</name> and <name>Grotius</name>, great admirers of the Fathers, regard this love as that of God or of Christ to us. <name>Wolfius</name> says, that all the Lutheran divines give this exposition. It is indeed impossible rightly to view the whole passage without seeing that this explanation is the true one. In verse 32, it is incontestably evident that God’s love to us is what is spoken of: then in verse 37, it is expressly said, “through him who loved us;” and the last verse seems sufficient to remove every possible doubt. The difficulty of <name>Barnes</name>, in thinking it “not conceivable how afflictions should have any tendency to alienate Christ’s love <hi type="italic">from us</hi>,” arises from a misconception: for when we speak of not being separated from the love of Christ, the obvious meaning is, that nothing can separate us from participating in the effects of his love, that He, on account of his love, will sustain us under the greatest trials, and make “us more than conquerors.” The substance of what is here said, is contained in the last clause of <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.32">Romans 8:32</reference>, — “How shall he not with him also freely give us all things?” It was the assurance of this truth that the Apostle obviously intended to convey. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114605" type="x-p"/> </note> but this comment may be easily disproved by the whole tenor of Paul’s reasoning; and Paul himself will presently remove all doubt by defining more clearly what this love is.<div eID="gen114604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114606" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Tribulation, or distress</hi>,<hi type="italic"> or persecution?</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> The pronoun masculine which he used at the beginning of the verse, contains a hidden power: for when he might have adopted the neuter gender and said — “What shall separate us?” etc., he preferred ascribing personality to things without life, and for this end, — that he might send forth with us into the contest as many champions as there are of temptations to try our faith.<div eID="gen114606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114607" type="x-p"/>But these three things have this difference: <hi type="italic">tribulation</hi> includes every kind of trouble or evil; <hi type="italic">distress</hi> is an inward feeling, when difficulties reduce us to such an extremity, so that we know not what course to pursue. Such was the anxiety of Abraham and of Lot, when one was constrained to expose his wife to the danger of prostitution, and the other, his daughters; for being brought to straits and being perplexed, they found no way of escape. <hi type="italic">Persecution</hi> properly denotes the tyrannical violence by which the children of God were undeservedly harassed by the ungodly. Now though Paul denies in <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.8">2 Corinthians 4:8</reference>, that the children of God are reduced to straits, <foreign xml:lang="el">στενοχωρεῖσθαι</foreign>, he does not yet disagree with himself; for he does not simply make them to be exempt from anxious solicitude, but he means that they are delivered from it, as also the examples of Abraham and Lot testify.<div eID="gen114607" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.35" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114602" osisID="Rom.8.35" type="section"/>
entries.5d409ec21cf50594878b83d492bc7ed854eb7a8f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.36" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.8.36" sID="gen114608" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">36.</hi> <hi type="italic">As it is written</hi>, <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> This testimony adds no small weight to the subject; for he intimates, that the dread of death is so far from being a reason to us for falling away, that it has been almost ever the lot of God’s servants to have death as it were present before their eyes. It is indeed probable, that in that Psalm the miserable oppression of the people under the tyranny of Antiochus is described; for it is expressly said, that the worshippers of God were cruelly treated, for no other reason but through hatred to true religion. There is also added a remarkable protestation, that they had not departed from the covenant of God; which Paul, I think, had especially in view. It is no objection that the saints there complain of a calamity which then unusually pressed on them; for since they show, that they were oppressed with so many evils, having before testified their innocence, an argument is hence fitly drawn, that it is no new thing for the Lord to permit his saints to be undeservedly exposed to the cruelty of the ungodly. But this is not done except for their good; for the Scripture teaches us, that it is alien to the righteousness of God to destroy the just with the wicked, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.23">Genesis 18:23</reference>); but that, on the contrary, it is meet for him to requite affliction to those who afflict, and rest to those who are afflicted. (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Thess.1.6 Bible:2Thess.1.9">2 Thessalonians 1:6, 9</reference>.) And then they affirm that they suffer for the Lord; and Christ pronounces them blessed who suffer for the sake of righteousness. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.10">Matthew 5:10</reference>.) By saying that they <hi type="italic">died daily</hi>, they intimated that death was so suspended over them, that their life differed but little from death.<div eID="gen114609" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.36" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114608" osisID="Rom.8.36" type="section"/>
entries.de309cf110cf0a5c60caab720908209ecfbf865c:
37. We do more than conquer, etc.; that is, we always struggle and emerge. I have retained the word used by Paul,
“Supervincimus“ — ὑπερνικῶμεν; Beza’s version is, amplius quam victores sumus;” Macknight’s, “we do more than overcome;” Schleusner gives this as one of his explanations, “plenissime vincimus — we most fully overcome.” Paul commonly uses ὑπὲρ in an enhansive sense; so the version may be, “we abundantly overcome,” as though he said, “We have strength given us which far exceeds the power of evils.” Some say that the faithful abundantly overcome, because they sustain no real loss, but like silver in the furnace, they lose only their dross; and not only so, but they also carry, as it were from the field of battle, chapter spoils — the fruits of holiness and righteousness. Hebrews 12:10,11. It is further said, that the victory will be this, — that Christ, who has loved them, will raise them from death and adorn them with that glory, with which all the evils of this life are not worthy to be compared.
Beza says, “Not only we are not broken down by so many evils nor despond, but we even glory in the cross.” — Ed.
though not commonly used by the Latins. It indeed sometimes happens that the faithful seem to succumb and to lie forlorn; and thus the Lord not only tries, but also humbles them. This issue is however given to them, — that they obtain the victory.
That they might at the same time remember whence this invincible power proceeds, he again repeats what he had said before: for he not only teaches us that God, because he loves us, supports us by his hand; but he also confirms the same truth by mentioning the love of Christ.
“Per eum qui dilexit nos — διὰ του ἀγαπήσαντος ἡμᾶς — through him who has loved us.” The aorist participle, says Wolfius, extends to every time, “who has loved and loves and will love us.” From the fact that believers are overcome by no calamities, he draws the inference, that God’s love is constant and most effectual, so that he is present with the distressed to give them courage, to strengthen their patience, and to moderate their calamities. See 1 Peter 5:10. — Ed.
And this one sentence sufficiently proves, that the Apostle speaks not here of the fervency of that love which we have towards God, but of the paternal kindness of God and of Christ towards us, the assurance of which, being thoroughly fixed in our hearts, will always draw us from the gates of hell into the light of life, and will sufficiently avail for our support.
Romans 8:38-39
38. For I am persuaded, that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor powers, nor things present, nor things to come,
38. Persuasus enim sum, quod neque mors, neque vita,
Neither death threatened by persecutors, nor life promised on recantation. — Ed.
neque angeli neque principatus, neque virtutes, neque principatus, neque virtutes, neque præasentia, neque futura,
39. Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
39. Neque altitudo, neque profunditas, neque ulla alia creatura, poterit nos dirimere a charitate Dei, Quæ est in Christo Iesu.
entries.cae378da0257a618b978108c31eb2ce878fbcc32: <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.38" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Rom.8.38" sID="gen114623" type="section"/> <div sID="gen114624" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">38.</hi> He is now carried away into hyperbolic expressions, that he might confirm us more fully in those things which are to be experienced. Whatever, he says, there is in life or in death, which seems capable of tearing us away from God, shall effect nothing; nay, the very angels, were they to attempt to overturn this foundation, shall do us no harm. It is no objection, that angels are ministering spirits, appointed for the salvation of the elect, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.1.14">Hebrews 1:14</reference>:) for Paul reasons here on what is impossible, as he does in <reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.8">Galatians 1:8</reference>; and we may hence observe, that all things ought to be deemed of no worth, compared with the glory of God, since it is lawful to dishonor even angels in vindicating his truth. <note n="279"> <div sID="gen114625" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic"> Some of the Fathers, </hi><name>Jerome</name><hi type="italic">,</hi> <name>Chrysostom</name>, etc., have taken the same view, regarding the Apostle as speaking of good angels, as it were, hypothetically, as in <reference osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.8">Galatians 1:8</reference>. But <name>Grotius</name>, and many others, consider <hi type="italic">evil </hi>angels to be meant. Probably, angels, without any regard to what they are, are intended. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114625" type="x-p"/> </note> Angels are also meant by <hi type="italic">principalities and powers</hi>, <note n="280"> <div sID="gen114626" type="x-p"/> <name>Grotius</name> considers the words as being the abstract for the concrete, Princes and Potentates; being called ἀρχαὶ, as some think, as being the first, the chief in authority, and δυνάμεις, as having power. “By these words,” says <name>Beza</name>, “Paul is wont to designate the character of spirits, — of the good in <reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.21">Ephesians 1:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Col.1.16">Colossians 1:16</reference>, — and of the bad in <reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.12 Bible:Col.2.15">Ephesians 6:12, Colossians 2:15</reference>.” Hence the probability is, that the words designate different ranks among angelic powers, without any reference to their character, whether good or evil. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114626" type="x-p"/> </note> and they are so called, because they are the primary instruments of the Divine power: and these two words were added, that if the word angels sounded too insignificant, something more might be expressed. But you would, perhaps, prefer this meaning, “Nor angels, and whatever powers there may be;” which is a mode of speaking that is used, when we refer to things unknown to us, and exceeding our capacities.<div eID="gen114624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114627" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Nor present things, nor future things,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> Though he speaks hyperbolically, yet he declares, that by no length of time can it be effected, that we should be separated from the Lord’s favor: and it was needful to add this; for we have not only to struggle with the sorrow which we feel from present evils, but also with the fear and the anxiety with which impending dangers may harass us. <note n="281"> <div sID="gen114628" type="x-p"/> “Neither the evils we now feel, nor those which may await us,” — <name>Grotius</name><hi type="italic">;</hi> rather, “Neither things which now exist, nor things which shall be.” — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114628" type="x-p"/> </note> The meaning then is, — that we ought not to fear, lest the continuance of evils, however long, should obliterate the faith of adoption.<div eID="gen114627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114629" type="x-p"/>This declaration is clearly against the schoolmen, who idly talk and say, that no one is certain of final perseverance, except through the gift of special revelation, which they make to be very rare. By such a dogma the whole faith is destroyed, which is certainly nothing, except it extends to death and beyond death. But we, on the contrary, ought to feel confident, that he who has begun in us a good work, will carry it on until the day of the Lord Jesus. <note n="282"> <div sID="gen114630" type="x-p"/> The words, “neither height nor depth,” are left unnoticed ὕψωμα. The first, says <name>Mede</name>, means prosperity, and the latter, adversity. <name>Grotius</name> regards what is meant as the <hi type="italic">height </hi>of honor, and the <hi type="italic">depth </hi>of disgrace. “Neither heaven nor hell,” say others; “neither heaven nor earth,” according to <name>Schleusner</name>. “Things in heaven and things on earth,” is the explanation of <name>Chrysostom</name> The first, ὕψωμα, is only found here and in <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.5">2 Corinthians 10:5</reference>. Like <foreign xml:lang="he">מרום</foreign> in Hebrew, it means what is high and elevated, and may, like that, sometimes signify heaven: and βάθος is not earth, but what is deeper; it means a deep soil, <reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.5">Matthew 13:5</reference>, — the deep sea, <reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.5.4">Luke 5:4</reference>, — and in the plural, things deep and inscrutable, <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.10">1 Corinthians 2:10</reference>; it may therefore be very properly taken here for hell.<div eID="gen114630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114631" type="x-p"/>That the words are to be thus taken seems probable from the gradation evident in the passage. In the first catalogue in <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.35">Romans 8:35</reference>, he mentions the evils arising from this world, its trials and its persecutions, and those ending in death. In the second, after repeating the utmost length to which worldly persecutors can go, “death or life,” he ascends the invisible world, and mentions angels, then their combined powers, then the powers which do and may exist, then both heaven and hell, and, that he might include everything, except the uncreated God himself, he finishes with the words, “nor any created thing.”<div eID="gen114631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen114632" type="x-p"/>The whole passage is sublime in an extraordinary degree. The contrast is the grandest that can be conceived. Here is the Christian, all weakness in himself, despised and trampled under foot by the world, triumphing over all existing, and all possible, and even impossible evils and opposition, having only this as his stay and support — that the God who has loved him, will never cease to love, keep, and defend him; yea, were everything created, everything except God himself, leagued against him and attempting his ruin. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen114632" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen114629" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Rom.8.38" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen114623" osisID="Rom.8.38" type="section"/>
entries.dc63fc201ccac53cfd96981441e055f925ff6ba6:
39. Which is in Christ, etc. That is, of which Christ is the bond; for he is the beloved Son, in whom the Father is well pleased. If, then, we are through him united to God, we may be assured of the immutable and unfailing kindness of God towards us. He now speaks here more distinctly than before, as he declares that the fountain of love is in the Father, and affirms that it flows to us from Christ.
CHAPTER 9
Romans 9:1-5
1. I say the truth in Christ, I lie not, my conscience also bearing me witness in the Holy Ghost,
1. Veritatem dico in Christo, non mentior, testimonium simul mihi reddente mea conscientia eum Spiri-tu sancto,
2. That I have great heaviness and continual sorrow in my heart.
2. Quod dolor sit mihi magnus, et assiduus cruciatus cordi meo:
3. For I could wish that myself were accursed from Christ for my brethren, my kinsmen according to the flesh:
3. Optarim enim ego ipse anathema esse a Christo pro fratribus meis, cognatis inquam meis secundum car-nem;
4. Who are Israelites; to whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises;
4. Qui sunt Israelitae, quorum est adoptio, et gloria, et testamenta, et legislatio, et cultus, et promissiones;
5. Whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen.
5. Quorum sunt Patres, et ex quibus est Christus secundum car-nem, qui est super omnia Deus bene-dictus in secula. Amen.

This is that which puts a weakness and inability upon the <ns0:hi>Law.</ns0:hi> The impoten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy of the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> is not from its self, but from the condition of the Subject with whom it hath to do. The <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> is weak to us, because we are weak to it: the Sun cannot give light to a blind eye, not from any impotency in its self, but meerly from the incapacity of the subject it shines upon.</ns0:note>, God send<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing his own Son <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To justifie and save fallen Man, was impossible for the Law to do; therefore God will find out another way, that shall do it effectually. What his own <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> cannot do, his own Son can; and therefore Him he will send.</ns0:note>, in the likness of sinful flesh <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Such flesh as sin hath made it now to be subject to many infirmities and weaknesses. Flesh in this clause carryes quite another sence, than it did in the first verse, and in the former part of this verse, then it doth in the following verse; there it is taken morally for the corrupt nature of man, here physically for the Humane Nature of Christ. The word likeness is to be linked, not with Flesh, but with sinful Flesh; he had true and real Flesh, but he had only the appearance and likeness of sinful Flesh. <ns0:hi>vid.</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.21. & 4.15. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 7.26. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 1.19.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note place="margin">
                     <ns0:hi>Or, by a <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> for sin.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> for sin <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either this clause is to be joyned to what goes before, and then the sence is, that God sent his Son in the likeness of sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Flesh, that he might take away <ns0:hi>Sin.</ns0:hi> Or, else it is joyned to what follows, and then there is an ellipsis in it. Something is cut off, or left out, which must be under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood. The margent of our Common Bibles insert the word Sacrifice. <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> by a Sacrifice for sin, or by a sin Offering <ns0:hi>he condemned Sin,</ns0:hi> &c. This ellipsis is usual in Scripture. <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53.10. <ns0:hi>When thou shalt make his Soul Sin</ns0:hi>; that is (as our translation renders it) an Offering for sin, <ns0:hi>Ezek</ns0:hi> 45.19. <ns0:hi>The Priest shall take of the Blood of the Sin,</ns0:hi> we read it of the Sin Offering. See the like in <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 4.8. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.21. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 10.6.</ns0:note>, condemned sin in the flesh <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Syriack</ns0:hi> reads it, <ns0:hi>in his Flesh.</ns0:hi> The meaning is, that God severely punished Sin, and inflicted the curse and penalty of it, that was due to us, in and upon the person of his own Son. God laid on him the iniquities of us all, and he bore them in his body upon a Tree. <ns0:hi>vid. Gal.</ns0:hi> 3.13. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.24.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">In this Verse is a farther proof of the main proposition in <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. There are two things in sin that may indanger us as to <ns0:hi>Condemnation,</ns0:hi> the power and guilt of it. As to the freeing us from the former, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> The power of sin, of that he had spoken in the foregoing verse; as to taking away the guilt of <ns0:hi>Sin,</ns0:hi> of that he speaks in this verse.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 That the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Here is another end of Gods sending his Son as be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore, it was that he might perfectly fulfil the Righteous<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of the Law in or for us, which for us our selves to do in our own Persons was utterly impossible. And yet upon which (as being imputed unto them, and accept<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed of God on our behalf) we shall be accounted Just and Righteous, as if we had done it our selves. Christs being a Sacrifice for sin was not sufficient to answer all the ends and demands of the Law; there must be doing of what it commanded, as well as suffering of what it threatned: Therefore Christ was sent for both, and both were ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />complished by him; and what he did and suffered is ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />counted unto us as if we had done and suffered it. This is the imputed Righteousness which was so often spoken of <ns0:hi>Chap.</ns0:hi> 4. and in reference to this he is said to be made Righteousness for us, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 1.30. and we are said to be the Righteousness of God in him, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 5.19. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 5.21.</ns0:note>, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">This was the description before of those that had Union with Christ, and exemption from Condemnation; and 'tis again set down as the description of those who partake of the Righteousness of Christ in this way of imputation; and 'tis added here again, to stave off all others from laying claim to this grace. None but holy walkers can warran<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tably apply Christs fulfilling or satisfying the Law to themselves, because Christ hath fulfilled the righteousness of the Law for us; none may infer there is nothing for us to do; we may live as we list: for though Christ hath fulfilled the Law in all respects, yet all those for whom he hath so done, or have benefit thereby, are, and must be such as <ns0:hi>walk not after the flesh, but after the spirit:</ns0:hi> for the opening of which terms, <ns0:hi>vid. v.</ns0:hi> 1.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 2.14.</ns0:note> they that are after the flesh <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That are carnal and unregenerate persons, in a meer natural estate.</ns0:note> do mind the things of the flesh <ns0:note n="s" place="margin">Either such things as are absolute<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly evil, and are called, <ns0:hi>The Iusts of the Flesh, Gal.</ns0:hi> 5.19, 20, 21. or else such things as are occasionally evil, as Riches, Honours, Pleasures, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> These are also called <ns0:hi>the things of the Flesh,</ns0:hi> and are such as carnal persons mind. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> They savour, affect, and take delight in them.</ns0:note>: but they that are after the Spirit <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> That are spiritual and regenerate, in whom the <ns0:hi>Spirit</ns0:hi> dwells.</ns0:note>, the things of the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> They mind Spiritual and Heavenly things, they relish them most of all. <ns0:hi>vid. Psal.</ns0:hi> 4.7. and 73.25.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 For <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.21. Gal. 6.8.</ns0:note> to be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>the mind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing or wisdom of the flesh.</ns0:hi> So <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7.</ns0:note> carnally minded <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> death <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To be of that temper before described, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. to mind and affect <ns0:hi>the things of the Flesh,</ns0:hi> doth cause <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>eath, or will end in it; the second or eternal death is chiefly intended.</ns0:note>, but to be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>the mind<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of the spirit</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> spiritually minded <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> to mind and savour the things of the Spirit, to find a sweetness and excellency therein, so as that the bent & inclination of the mind shall be there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> life and peace <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">It is the way to Eternal Life hereafter, and to a sound peace here, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 119.165. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3.17. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.16.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">In this verse we have an account of the different end of those that are <ns0:hi>carnal</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>spiritual,</ns0:hi> as in the former we had a description of their different carriage and dispositi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:420" />7 Because <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Neither can the <ns0:hi>carnal man</ns0:hi> look for any bet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter issue, <ns0:hi>Because a carnal mind is enmity against God.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> the carnal mind <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> enmity <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">He doth not say it is an <ns0:hi>Enemy,</ns0:hi> but in the abstract, it is <ns0:hi>enmity,</ns0:hi> which heightens and intends the sence; an <ns0:hi>enemy</ns0:hi> may be reconciled; as <ns0:hi>Esau</ns0:hi> was to <ns0:hi>Iacob</ns0:hi>; but <ns0:hi>Enmity</ns0:hi> cannot be reconciled, as black may be made white, but blackness cannot.</ns0:note> against God: for it is not subject to the law of God, neither indeed can be <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">This is rendred as a reason of the foregoing assertion, and it is taken from the property of <ns0:hi>enmity.</ns0:hi> Those that are at <ns0:hi>enmity,</ns0:hi> cross each others wills, and won't submit to one another: and <ns0:hi>the carnal mind is</ns0:hi> rebellious in the highest degree against the will of <ns0:hi>God,</ns0:hi> unless it be changed and renewed; it is impossible it should be otherwise. There is in it a moral impotency to obedience. <ns0:hi>vid. Iohn</ns0:hi> 8.43. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.14.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 So then <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This verse is a consectary, or it follows from that which went before.</ns0:note> they that are in the flesh <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Not they which are married, as a Pope once expounded it. The next verse refells such an absurd conception; but they that are carnal and unre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />generate, the same with those, who in <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 5. are said to be after the <ns0:hi>Flesh.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not please God <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Neither they, nor any thing they do, is pleasing unto him: their best works are dead works, and Silken sins, (as one expresseth it) it must be understood with this limitation, so long as they con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tinue in such a State. <ns0:hi>vid. Psal.</ns0:hi> 54.5. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 11.6.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 But ye <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Here he applies what he had laid down more ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nerally to the believing <ns0:hi>Romans</ns0:hi> in particular.</ns0:note> are not in the flesh, but in the Spirit <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e. Not after the Flesh, but after the Spirit</ns0:hi> (as in <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 5. or <ns0:hi>not car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nally, but Spiritually minded.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, if <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Conjunction here is <ns0:hi>causal</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>conditional</ns0:hi>; it may be rendred, seeing that, or forasmuch as. <ns0:hi>vid. v.</ns0:hi> 17. & 31. 2 <ns0:hi>Thes.</ns0:hi> 1.6.</ns0:note> so be that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 3.16.</ns0:note> the Spirit of God dwell in you <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>The Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit of God dwells in the regenerate,</ns0:hi> not only by the immen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sity of his presence, so he is every where and in all things: but by the presence and efficacy of his grace; the indwel<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ling of the Spirit in Believers, denotes two things. 1. His ruling in them; where a man dwells as Lord, there he doth command and bear rule. 2. His abiding in them, and that for ever. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 14.16.</ns0:note>. Now if any man have not the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 3.34. Phil. 1.19. 1 Pet 1.11.</ns0:note> Spirit of Christ, he is none of his <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">If he hath <ns0:hi>not the same Spirit</ns0:hi> which in the forgoing verse is called, <ns0:hi>the Spirit of God</ns0:hi>; it is called, <ns0:hi>the Spirit of Christ</ns0:hi>; because it proceeds from him, and is procured by him. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 14.26. and 16.7. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.6. When he saith such a one <ns0:hi>is none of Christs</ns0:hi>; he means, that he doth not peculiarly belong to Christ, he hath no special interest in him, is no true Member of him. As a Merchant sets his Seal upon his Goods, so doth Christ his Spirit upon his followers, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 1.13.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 And if Christ <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Before, he said the <ns0:hi>Spirit of God and Christ dwelt in them</ns0:hi>; here Christ himself. <ns0:hi>Christ dwells in Believers by his Spirit.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> in you, the body <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>body</ns0:hi> some understand the corrupt and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />regenerate part in the godly, as if that were as good as dead in them. But others take the word in its proper signification, and think no more is meant thereby than that the <ns0:hi>Bodies</ns0:hi> even of <ns0:hi>Believers,</ns0:hi> are mortal <ns0:hi>Bodies</ns0:hi>; so they are called in the next verse. They are subject to death as the <ns0:hi>bodies</ns0:hi> of other men.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> dead because of sin; but the Spirit <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> life <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Some by <ns0:hi>Spirit</ns0:hi> here do un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand the <ns0:hi>Spirit of God,</ns0:hi> and he is life; that is, he will quicken and raise up your <ns0:hi>bodies</ns0:hi> again to an immor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tal life. Others by <ns0:hi>Spirit</ns0:hi> do understand the Souls, yet not simply and absolutly considered, but as renewed by grace; that is life, or that doth live: it lives a life of <ns0:hi>Grace</ns0:hi> here, and it shall live a life of <ns0:hi>Glory</ns0:hi> hereafter.</ns0:note>, because of righteousness <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By <ns0:hi>Righteousness,</ns0:hi> here understand, either imputed <ns0:hi>Righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness,</ns0:hi> which gives us a right and title to <ns0:hi>Salvation</ns0:hi>; or inherent <ns0:hi>Righteousness,</ns0:hi> which is a necessary condition re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quired in every Person, that shall indeed be saved. The Sum is, if you be Christians indeed, though your <ns0:hi>bodies</ns0:hi> dye, yet your <ns0:hi>Souls</ns0:hi> shall live, and that for ever; and your dead <ns0:hi>bodies</ns0:hi> shall not finally perish, but shall certainly be raised again; so it follows in the next verse.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11. But if the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus from the dead <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">A Periphrasis of <ns0:hi>God the Father.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Son</ns0:hi> raised him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.19. and 10.18. and yet the <ns0:hi>Father</ns0:hi> is said here to <ns0:hi>raise</ns0:hi> him from the dead. <ns0:hi>vid.</ns0:hi> notes on <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.4.</ns0:note> dwell in you <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 6.4, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 1 Cor. 6.14. 2 Cor. 4.14<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Eph. 2.5.</ns0:note>; he that raised up Christ from the dead, shall also quick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />en your mortal bodies <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Raise</ns0:hi> them from a State of Mortality. & all the attendants to a glorious immortal life.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>because of his Spirit.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, by his Spirit that dwelleth in you <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> If you are sanctified by the Spirit, you shall be raised up by the Spirit also, as Christ was. The wicked also shall be raised at the last day. But the <ns0:hi>Righteous</ns0:hi> shall be raised after a peculiar manner, they shall be raised as by the Almighty Power of God; so by vertue of their Union with Christ as his members, and by vertue of their relation to the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit as his Temples. They only shall partake of a <ns0:hi>Resur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rection,</ns0:hi> that is desirable and beneficial to them. Therefore 'tis called Emphatically the <ns0:hi>Resurrection of the Iust,</ns0:hi> Luke 14.14. and these two are joyned together, as belonging one to the other; the Children of God, and the Children of the Resurrection, <ns0:hi>Luke.</ns0:hi> 20.36.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 Therefore <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This illative particle sends us to the things before delivered. <ns0:hi>q. d.</ns0:hi> Seeing we are not in the Flesh, but have the Spirit of God dwelling in us; not only sanctifying and enlivening our souls for the present, but raising and quick<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ening our bodies for time to come, <ns0:hi>therefore we are not Debtors,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> brethren, we are debtors, not to the flesh, to live after the flesh <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e. We are not Debtors to Sin,</ns0:hi> or the cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rupt and sinful nature that is in us. We owe it no ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vice, there is nothing due to it from Believers, but blows, and the blew eye that the Apostle gave it. The Anti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thesis is omitted, but it is necessarily implyed and under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stood; and that is, <ns0:hi>That we are debters to the Spirit, to live and walk after it.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Eternally, and never partake of the glorious Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />surrection before spoken of. The Godly themselves need this caution; they must not think, that because they are elected and justified, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> that therefore they may do and live as they list.</ns0:note>: but if ye through the Spirit <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> By the grace and assistance of the Spirit.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Eph. 4.22<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Col. 3.5.</ns0:note>, do mortifie <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e</ns0:hi> Kill and put to death. Tis not enough to forbear the actings of Sin, but we must kill and cru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cifie it. Sin may be left upon many considerations, and yet not mortified.</ns0:note> the deeds of the body <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Evil deeds are called the deeds of the body, because the body is so instrumental in the doing thereof. There are some, that by body here do understand the corrupt nature, the same that before in many places he calls the flesh: this was called, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 6.6. <ns0:hi>the body of Sin,</ns0:hi> and here 'tis called <ns0:hi>the body.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, ye shall live <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> Eternally. See a parallel-place, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 6.22. <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 6.8. <ns0:hi>vid. v.</ns0:hi> 6.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 For <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">This proves the latter part of the foregoing verse, such as by the Spirit do mortifie Sin, shall live; for they are the Sons of God; and that appears, because they are led by the Spirit of God.</ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gal. 5.1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> as many as are led <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He doth not say as many as live by the Spirit, but as one led by the Spirit; to shew (sayes one) that the Spirit must be the guide & ruler of our Life, as the Pilot is of the Ship, and as a Rider is of his Horse. The Phrase is borrowed (sayes another) either from those which are guided and directed as a blind man in his way; or from those, who wanting strength of their own, are borne and carryed of others: so we are both wayes led by the Spirit, for we can neither see our way, unless the Spirit directs us; nor have we strength to walk in it, unless the Spirit assist and draw us along. The Spirit leads and draws us irresistably and necessarily, and yet not violently or against our wills; though we were unwilling before, yet we are made willing afterwards; so willing, that we desire and pray to be led by the Spirit. <ns0:hi>vid.</ns0:hi> and 25.5: <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 143.10. <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 1.4.</ns0:note> by the Spirit of God, they are the Sons of God.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 For <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">This verse proves the former, that we <ns0:hi>are led by the Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rit of God,</ns0:hi> and are his Children, and that by an effect of the Spirit in them, which is to enable them to call <ns0:hi>God Father.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 2.<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>

                  </ns0:note> it self beareth witness <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The <ns0:hi>Spirit of Adoption</ns0:hi> doth not only excite us to call upon <ns0:hi>God</ns0:hi> as our <ns0:hi>Father,</ns0:hi> but it doth ascertain and assure us (as before) that we are <ns0:hi>His Children.</ns0:hi> And this it doth not by an outward voice, as <ns0:hi>God the Father to Iesus Christ</ns0:hi>; nor by an Angel, as to <ns0:hi>Daniel</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Vir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gin Mary</ns0:hi>; but by an inward and secret suggestion, whereby he raiseth our hearts to this perswasion, that <ns0:hi>God is our Father and we are his Children.</ns0:hi> This is not the Testimony of the Graces and Operations of the <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> but of the <ns0:hi>Spirit</ns0:hi> it self. Conceives it thus; A mans own Spirit doth witness to him his Adoption, he finds in him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self upon diligent search and examination, the manifest signes and tokens thereof. This Testimony is not alike in all <ns0:hi>Believers,</ns0:hi> nor in any one of them at all times; it is better felt than ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed. <ns0:hi>He witnesseth to our Spirit</ns0:hi> (so some read it) by a distinct and immediate testimony, <ns0:hi>and witnesseth with our Spirit</ns0:hi> (so the word properly signifies) by a conjunctive and concurrent testimony.</ns0:note> with our spirit, that we are the children of God.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="19">19 For the earnest expectation of the crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ture <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">This word is four times used in this and the three following verses, only in the 22. <ns0:hi>verse,</ns0:hi> tis rendred <ns0:hi>Creation</ns0:hi>; that is the subject of which all that followeth is predicated. By the <ns0:hi>Creature</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Creation</ns0:hi> (and <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. the whole <ns0:hi>Creation</ns0:hi> or every <ns0:hi>Creature</ns0:hi>) is meant all mankind, both <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Gentiles,</ns0:hi> and especially the lat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter. <ns0:hi>vid. Mar.</ns0:hi> 16.15. there Christ gives it in Commission to preach the Gospel to every <ns0:hi>Creature</ns0:hi>; 'tis the same word. And in 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.13. They are commanded <ns0:hi>to sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mit themselves to every Ordinance of Man.</ns0:hi> In the Origi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal it is to <ns0:hi>every humane Creature,</ns0:hi> the same word which is in the Text before us; he mean<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the <ns0:hi>Gentile</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Heathen Magistrates</ns0:hi> in <ns0:hi>Authority</ns0:hi> over them. In the Scripture the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> are sometimes called the <ns0:hi>World, chap.</ns0:hi> 11.12, 15. and sometimes the <ns0:hi>Creature</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Creation.</ns0:hi> 2. By the <ns0:hi>Creature</ns0:hi> is meant <ns0:hi>the whole World</ns0:hi> with all the <ns0:hi>Creatures</ns0:hi> therein, or the whole Frame and body of the <ns0:hi>Creation.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Creature</ns0:hi> in this sence by a <ns0:hi>Prosopopeia</ns0:hi> is here spo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken of as a <ns0:hi>rational Person</ns0:hi>; it is usual with the Spirit of God in Scripture, to fasten upon unreasonable <ns0:hi>Creatures,</ns0:hi> such expressions, as are proper only to those that are reasonable. <ns0:hi>vid. Psal.</ns0:hi> 96.11, 12. <ns0:hi>Hab.</ns0:hi> 2.11. <ns0:hi>Iames</ns0:hi> 5.4.                <ns0:p n="20">20 For the creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">If these words be understood of the World, and all the <ns0:hi>Creatures</ns0:hi> therein contained, then they shew the <ns0:hi>Creatures present condition,</ns0:hi> it is subject to vanity, and that first in regard of its <ns0:hi>insufficiency,</ns0:hi> it falling short of that for which it was first created and ordained; then a thing is said to be vain, when it doth not answer or reach its proper end: Or in respect of its <ns0:hi>Transitoriness</ns0:hi> and uncertainty, of which see, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7.31. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 1.11, 12. 1 <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 2.17. The next verse tells us it is subject to the <ns0:hi>Bondage of Corruption</ns0:hi> as well as Vanity. Now this must needs be an unwilling subjection, therefore 'tis here said it is not subject will<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ingly. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> of its one accord, or of its proper Instinct and Inclination; what the Will is in those that are rational, the Inclination is in these things that are natural; how comes it then into this condition? The next clause tells us, it is by reason of him who hath subjected the same in <ns0:hi>Hope.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>, but by reason of him who hath subjected <ns0:hi>the same</ns0:hi> in hope <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> God for the Sin of Man hath curst the <ns0:hi>Creature,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Subjected</ns0:hi> it to vanity and corruption. <ns0:hi>vid. Gen.</ns0:hi> 3.17. and 4.12. <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 26.19, 20. And though he hath done this, yet there is ground to expect and hope that the Creature shall return again to its former estate where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />in it was created; that it shall be delivered and restored into a better condition, as in the next verse. Those that by the Creature understand the <ns0:hi>Gentile</ns0:hi> World, give a dif<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferent interpretation of these words; they say that the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> are made subject to Vanity. <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> To Idolatry or a Vain Superstitious Worship. (Idols are called Vanities, <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 14.15.) or to a miserable wretched estate that (as <ns0:hi>Hesychius</ns0:hi> notes) is the import of the word Vanity. And this not so much of their own accord, or by their own free choice, but by the power and malice of Satan, to whom they are justly given up of God, he rules in their hearts, carries them captive at his will, subjects them to all vil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lany and misery. And it is reasonable to suppose of these poor Heathens, that they are willing to be rescued (at least some, and a considerable number of them) from under this vanity and slavery (as it is said, v. 22.) <ns0:hi>Q.</ns0:hi> But if he that thus subjects them be the Devil, how is he said to do this in hope? <ns0:hi>A.</ns0:hi> These words in hope belong to the end of the former Verse; all the rest of this verse be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing read or included in a <ns0:hi>Parenthesis. q. d.</ns0:hi> The Creature attends the manifestations of the Sons of God in Hope. Mean while it is subject to Vanity, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="21">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:421" />21 Because the creature it self also shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption, into the glorious liberty of the children of God <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">If this verse be understood of the Heavens, and the Earth, and the things therein, the meaning is, that the Creatures in their kind, and according to their capacity, shall be partakers of that Liberty and freedom, which in the Children of God, is accompanied with unspeakable Glory, they shall not partake with<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> the Saints in Glory, but of that Liberty which in the Saints hath great Glory attending it, and superadded to it. The Creature at the day of Judgment shall be restored (as before) to that condition of liberty which it had in its first Creation; as when it was made at first, it was free from all Vanity, Bondage and Corruption, so it shall be again at the time of the general Resurrection. <ns0:hi>vid. Act.</ns0:hi> 3.19, 21. 2 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 3.13. Those that by the Creation, would understand the <ns0:hi>Gentile</ns0:hi> World, give the sense of this verse. That the very Heathens also shall by the Gospel and Grace of Christ be rescued from those courses of Sin and Corruption, to which they have been long enslaved, into that glorious condition not only of free men, redeemed by Christ out of their bondage to sin and Satan, but even of the Sons of God to have right to his favour, and that never fading inheritance.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="22">22 For we know that the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>every creature.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> whole creation groaneth, and travaileth in <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>in pains of Child birth.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> pain together un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />til now <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">If here again the Heavens and the Earth, with what is therein be understood, then the Apostle farther enlargeth upon their present State and Condition; before they wait<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed and expected deliverance, now they groan and travail in pain. They also are metaphorical Expressions; one is taken for a Man, who hath upon him a heavy burthen, another from a Woman that is near her delivery, and this they do until now, <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> From the Fall of <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> to this present day. They that understand the words of the <ns0:hi>Gentile</ns0:hi> World, thus interpret them. We the Apostles and Ministers of Jesus Christ, do find by experience, that the <ns0:hi>Gentiles</ns0:hi> are very forward to receive the Gospel, when they hear it, whilst the <ns0:hi>Iewes</ns0:hi> generally reject it. The <ns0:hi>Gentile</ns0:hi> World is as it were in pangs of travail, ever since Christs time till now, ready to bring forth Sons and Daughters to God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="34">34. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 34.29.</ns0:note> Who <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> he that condemneth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">As none can Accuse the <ns0:hi>Elect of God,</ns0:hi> so much less can any Condemn them, <ns0:hi>vid. ver.</ns0:hi> 1.</ns0:note>? <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> Christ that dyed <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">And 'tis He that is the Judge, and must <ns0:hi>condemn them,</ns0:hi> if they be <ns0:hi>condemned.</ns0:hi> His <ns0:hi>Death</ns0:hi> frees them from <ns0:hi>Condemnation</ns0:hi>; thereby he hath made a sufficient Attonement and Satisfaction for all their Sins: And that which hath long ago satisfied in Heaven, for the Sins of all the <ns0:hi>Elect,</ns0:hi> may very well serve to satisfy the <ns0:hi>Heart</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Conscience</ns0:hi> of a <ns0:hi>Believing sinner</ns0:hi> here on Earth.                <ns0:p n="35">35.                <ns0:p n="36">36.                      <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> We are designed for Destruction. Our Enemies make account they can Destroy us, as Men do Sheep, that they have by them in the Slaughter-house. They were all shut up in one House together, as in a Sheepfold: An Executioner comes in, and among them takes one, and blind-folds him with a Muffler about his Eyes, and so leadeth him forth to a larger Place, where he Commandeth him to Kneel down; which being done, he cutteth his Throat, and so leaveth him half Dead; and taking his Butchers Knife and Muffler, all of gore Blood, he cometh again to the rest, and so leading them one af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter another, he dispatcheth them to the number of <ns0:hi>Eighty Eight,</ns0:hi> no otherwise than a Butcher doth his Sheep. <ns0:hi>Fox</ns0:hi> his <ns0:hi>Act. & Monum.</ns0:hi>

                     <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> In <ns0:hi>Tribulation, Distress,</ns0:hi> &c, as before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 35.</ns0:note>, we are more than conquerors <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Or we overcome. We <ns0:hi>Conquer,</ns0:hi> when we our selves are <ns0:hi>conquered</ns0:hi>; We <ns0:hi>conquer</ns0:hi> by those, which are wont to <ns0:hi>con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quer</ns0:hi> others; we beat our Enemies with their own Wea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pons. The meaning seems to be this, The Devil aims in all the Sufferings of God's Children, to Draw them off from Christ, to make them Murmur, Despair, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> But in this he is defeated, and disappointed; for God Inspires his Children with such a Generous and Noble <ns0:hi>Spirit,</ns0:hi> that <ns0:hi>Sufferings</ns0:hi> abate not their Zeal and Patience, but rather increase it. <ns0:hi>We Christians laugh at your cruelty, and grow the more resolute,</ns0:hi> said one of <ns0:hi>Iulian</ns0:hi>'s Nobles to him.</ns0:note>, through him that loved us <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">A short Description of Christ, together with a Reason of a Christians Success. The <ns0:hi>conquest</ns0:hi> he hath over Sin, and o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ver Sufferings also, is not from himself, or his own Strength, but from Christ, <ns0:hi>&c. vid. chap.</ns0:hi> 7.24, 25. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 15.57. 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.14. 2 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 4.17.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
